preprints.title: Aging activates latent enhancers that can be reversed withexercise
preprints.abstract: Aging profoundly alters the genome's regulatory landscape, but the properties of age-acquired enhancers, including how they are selected and sustained in aged animals are unclear. We used single-cell multiomics in the mouse heart to identify age-responsive cis-regulatory elements and endurance exercise to understand which of these elements can be attenuated. Aging increased AP-1 engagement at more than 100,000 regulatory loci across cardiac cell types. Exercise opposed most of these gains. Despite low endogenous accessibility, age-gained enhancer sequences drove reporter activity comparable to stable elements, revealing substantial latent transcriptional potential. Local sequence features distinguished responsiveness to aging and exercise. Reporter perturbations implicated sequence outside the AP-1 core, and mutagenesis localized informative positions to dispersed segments of dynamic enhancers. These enhancers were IL-1-sensitive and were preferentially responsive to neutralization of the cytokine in vivo. AP-1 inhibition further opposed age-associated transcription. Together, these findings support a model in which aging engages latent cell-type specific enhancers that are sustained in an active state by ongoing trans signaling. Aging therefore changes the deployment of existing regulatory information, while the acquired activity remains responsive to changes in signaling even in old age.

preprints.title: Biological Signaling Pathways Associated with Late Tendon Development in Chicken Embryos and Their Dependence on Mechanical Stimulation
preprints.abstract: During embryonic and neonatal development, tendons exhibit rapid changes in mechanics and structure, including increases in collagen content, crosslinking, and fibril length. These functional and structural changes are partly dependent on mechanical stimulation. However, the specific mechanobiological mechanisms driving these changes remain poorly understood. The objective of this study was to identify the potential biological mechanisms and pathways driving tendon maturation into load-bearing materials using an embryonic chick model. Using bulk RNA sequencing, gene set enrichment analysis, and transcription factor analysis, we produced a transcriptomic profile of chick hindlimb tendons during late embryonic development (E16, E18, and E20) and tendons from rigid and flaccid paralysis-treated embryos. Additionally, we assessed the results from two differential expression analysis models to improve the replicability of our findings. Our results suggest that the largest transcriptomic response occurs between embryonic day 16 and 20, and that among paralysis conditions, rigid paralysis produces the greatest effect relative to controls. Across development, we found positive enrichment in processes related to mechanotransduction, extracellular matrix remodeling, cell adhesion, and contractility, and identified candidate pathways upregulated with development, including TGF-{beta}, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, Hippo, circadian rhythm, and focal adhesion signaling. In paralysis-treated embryos, our data suggest impairment in extracellular matrix remodeling and mechanotransduction events. Specifically, we found that both modes of paralysis are associated with a cellular stress response and downregulation of WNT signaling. Together, our findings identify candidate mechanotransduction pathways that are associated with late tendon maturation and altered by paralysis, which may inform tendon tissue engineering and regenerative approaches.

last_author.name: Szczesny, S. E.
last_author.affiliation: The Pennsylvania State University

preprints.title: DPYD links glial lipids and myelination to sleep duration
preprints.abstract: The regulation of sleep is heritable and conserved across species1,2, but the governing genetic mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the role of DPYD--which encodes the pyrimidine catabolic enzyme, dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase--in sleep. Using a cross-species approach, we show that DPYD and its orthologs act specifically in glia to promote sleep through the regulation of brain lipids. In mouse and zebrafish, we find that DPYD orthologs are enriched in oligodendrocyte lineage cells, and their loss reduces myelination and sleep independent of DPYDs established role in uracil catabolism to {beta}-alanine. Genetic and pharmacological manipulations of myelin in zebrafish show that altering myelination is sufficient to perturb sleep duration. In Drosophila, which lack myelin, we find that the DPYD ortholog acts in ensheathing glia to promote sleep through formation of glial lipid droplets, a proposed evolutionary precursor to myelin. Furthermore, a human GWAS-identified sleep variant2 resides in a conserved cis-regulatory element that selectively contacts the promoter of DPYD within oligodendrocytes, connecting the human genetic association to oligodendrocyte-specific control of DPYD. Together, these results identify a deeply conserved role for glial lipids in sleep regulation and establish DPYD as a mechanistic link between myelin biology and sleep.

preprints.title: Development of a multi-organ single-cell atlas of systemic sclerosis reveals shared and tissue-specific pathogenic pathways.
preprints.abstract: Objectives: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a multi-organ autoimmune disease for which no broadly effective disease-modifying treatment exists. We developed an integrated multi-organ single-cell atlas of SSc to identify shared and organ specific disease-associated transcriptional programmes and potential therapeutic targets. Methods: We integrated single-cell RNA-sequencing data from skin, lung, synovium, and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (six studies, 401,902 cells, 90 individuals) using Harmony. Pseudobulk differential expression and gene set enrichment analysis were performed at the tissue cell-compartment, cell-type, and subpopulation levels, including independent reclustering of lymphoid, myeloid and fibroblast populations. Results: Disease-associated transcriptional programmes showed marked tissue dependence, even within the same cell lineage, highlighting the importance of organ-specific mechanisms in SSc. Nevertheless, recurrent extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling programmes were identified in lung, skin and synovium, and interferon signalling programmes in skin, synovium and peripheral blood mononuclear cells, across immune and fibroblast cell populations. Although no subpopulation was exclusive to SSc, a shared myofibroblast subpopulation expressing SFRP2, COL1A1, POSTN, ACTA2, and COMP was identified across lung, skin, and synovium. In addition, perivascular and mitotic fibroblast subpopulations exhibited both profibrotic and inflammatory signatures, including interferon- and IL-2-related signalling programmes. Conclusions: SSc is characterised by two complementary axes: a tissue-dependent cellular programme and a recurrent fibrotic and interferon-associated signature extending across multiple organs and cell populations. These findings are consistent with current organ-based therapeutic approaches while highlighting interferon signalling as a potential multi-organ therapeutic target. The resulting interactive single-cell atlas provides a resource for investigating shared and organ-specific disease mechanisms and guiding future therapeutic research.

preprints.title: Few-shot regulatory sequence design with a genomic language model
preprints.abstract: A central challenge in generative biology is translating knowledge learned from natural sequences and experiments into designs with desired functions. In-context learning (ICL) is an emergent capability of large language models that allows them to adapt to new tasks from a few examples without additional training, enabling these models to become general-purpose learners. Here, we show that the genome language model, Evo 2, exhibits generative ICL in biological sequence design. Prompting with just tens of examples conditions Evo 2 to generate novel and diverse regulatory DNA sequences without any additional training. Mechanistic analysis suggests that genomic ICL may originate from induction, similar to phenomena observed in natural language. Reinforcement learning leveraging sequence-to-function models as experiment-derived rewards further strengthens ICL. We first validate this approach by generating enhancers that drive cell-type-specific gene expression in three human cell lines. Extending this approach in vivo, enhancers designed using human regulatory element data selectively label layer 5 extratelencephalic neurons in the mouse cortex with high specificity and stronger activity than existing enhancers. Our study provides evidence of emergent properties in genomic sequence models and introduces a promising approach for improving functional conditioning in generative biology.

last_author.name: Allen, W. E.
last_author.affiliation: Department of Chemical Engineering, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA

preprints.title: Homoplastic evolution of proximal podomere patterning across Arthropoda
preprints.abstract: The jointed arthropod leg is often credited as a key innovation spurring the evolutionary success of the phylum. Across lineages, each territory of the appendage has served as the substrate for myriad adaptations and structural innovations. While much of the available data has supported a conserved suite of transcription factors responsible for the initiation and patterning of the arthropod appendage, recent works have begun to highlight instances of lineage-specific shifts in expression dynamics, particularly amongst the chelicerates, correlated both with the emergence of novel structures and developmental system drift in the specification of plesiomorphic structures. These works confound efforts to align or homologize the leg segments across arthropod lineages, an effort already challenged by ground plan differences in segment number between the subphyla. An even more unusual architecture of leg segments occurs in sea spiders (Pycnogonida), which alone among Arthropoda are considered by systematists to bear three coxae (proximal segments), in contrast to the single coxa of the remaining arthropods. Here, we examined proximal podomere patterning in the developing appendages of a sea spider and an arachnid. We find that a particular spatial arrangement of Lim1 and SoxNeuro characterizes the developing coxa and trochanter of the harvestman Phalangium opilio (Opiliones) throughout appendage formation, with RNAi depletions of Lim1 yielding deletions of coxa and trochanter. Comparison of expression patterns across taxa shows that Lim1 and SoxNeuro have a similar spatial arrangement in the harvestman and sea spider, but these suggest conflicting interpretations of leg segment homology. We show that this is attributable to homoplastic patterns of evolution in SoxNeuro across Arthropoda. Expanding our surveys of prominent PD axis-patterning transcription factors supports additional instances of homoplasy in the domains of Sp6-9 and Irx2. The pervasiveness of homoplasy in gene expression patterns demands measured skepticism of homology statements and careful comparisons of multiple patterning genes, toward achieving falsifiability in the homology of structures.

preprints.title: Imbalance between RNA-binding proteins and the WAVE regulatory complex underlies the toxic gain-of-function effects of the CYFIP2 Arg87Cys variant in neurodevelopmental disorders
preprints.abstract: Pathogenic variants in cytoplasmic FMR1-interacting protein 2 (CYFIP2) cause neurodevelopmental disorders, with hotspot substitutions at arginine 87 (Arg87) associated with particularly severe symptoms. CYFIP2 functions both as a component of the WAVE (Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein family verprolin-homologous protein) regulatory complex (WRC), regulating the actin cytoskeleton, and as an interactor of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) involved in mRNA processing/translation. Although Arg87 variants reduce CYFIP2 protein stability, heterozygous knock-in mice carrying Arg87Cys (Cyfip2+/R87C) show markedly more severe phenotypes than heterozygous knockout (Cyfip2+/-) mice, supporting a toxic gain-of-function mechanism. However, how the dual roles of CYFIP2 contribute to this mechanism remains unclear. To address this, we examined Cyfip2+/R87C mice at postnatal week 7, before overt neuronal loss and gliosis, focusing on the progressive dispersion of hippocampal cornu ammonis 1 (CA1) pyramidal neurons, a phenotype absent in Cyfip2+/- mice. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing suggested candidate alterations related to translation and cell adhesion/migration in CA1 pyramidal neurons. Complementarily, human embryonic kidney 293T cells expressing CYFIP2 Arg87Cys showed defects in proliferation and morphology, accompanied by altered expression of cell adhesion-related genes. Quantitative proteomic analysis of the CA1 region uncovered an imbalance between CYFIP2-associated protein networks, characterized by increased RBPs and reduced WRC components. Phosphoproteomic analysis further revealed altered phosphorylation of synaptic and translational regulators. Consistently, whole-cell recordings and biocytin-based morphological analyses showed increased frequency of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents and altered dendritic morphology in Cyfip2+/R87C CA1 pyramidal neurons, most prominently in the more severely dispersed deep-layer neurons. Moreover, the cell adhesion molecule Eph receptor A3 was reduced, possibly as a result of RBP dysregulation. Together, these findings suggest that an imbalance between RBP- and WRC-associated pathways underlies the gain-of-function effects of CYFIP2 Arg87Cys and contributes to early neuronal phenotypes, most notably CA1 layer dispersion. This mechanism, distinct from CYFIP2 haploinsufficiency, supports allele-specific therapeutic strategies for Arg87 variants.

preprints.title: LabWeaver: reliable agentic data analysis grounded in laboratory knowled
preprints.abstract: Agentic systems powered by large language models are rapidly automating biological data analysis. However, their reliability remains questionable because they often overlook experimental context, such as disease domain and experimental protocol. Existing agentic systems organize context around individual users and projects, whereas research is organized around laboratories whose projects share experimental context. As a result, experimental context learned in one project remains unavailable to related projects. We introduce LabWeaver, an agentic data analysis framework with a laboratory-organized architecture of three tiers: laboratory, user and project. Further, LabWeaver distills experimental context into laboratory memory and skills, which are shared across users and projects after human-gated review. To isolate the contribution of experimental context, we analyzed a synovial sarcoma single-cell RNA-seq dataset in two sessions that differed only in whether laboratory memory and skills were available. The context-free session lost the fusion reporter at read alignment and misannotated the tumor cells. In contrast, the context-enabled session recovered reporter expression and resolved five fusion-anchored tumor cell states.

preprints.title: Lineage tracing in rhabdoid tumor organoids and orthotopic xenografts reveals convergent transcriptional states
preprints.abstract: Malignant rhabdoid tumors (MRTs) are aggressive pediatric malignancies driven by loss of a single SWI/SNF subunit in an otherwise near-silent genome, yet they display extensive transcriptional heterogeneity. Whether this heterogeneity reflects the outgrowth of transcriptionally distinct clones, or states adopted independently of lineage, is unknown. Here we combined lentiviral lineage barcoding with single-cell RNA sequencing in two patient-derived renal MRT organoid models, followed through long-term in vitro culture and in a novel orthotopic xenograft setting. In both modalities, tumors and cultures became progressively restricted to a small number of lineages, and the clones that expanded were transcriptionally distinct from one another. Decomposing into gene expression programs showed that some transcriptional states were used broadly across lineages while others were confined to a few, and that lineages expanding independently, in separate cultures and separate animals, converged on the same restricted states. Individual lineages generally maintained their transcriptional identity across passaging and across anatomical sites, including in metastases, which arose from clones already expanded in the matched primary tumor. Which lineages came to dominate, however, differed between animals given the same starting population. Clonal outcome is therefore variable while the transcriptional states available to a tumor are drawn from a constrained and recurring repertoire.

preprints.title: Mechanistic gene-regulation-based trajectory inference with bowside
preprints.abstract: While single-cell RNA sequencing enables the in-depth study of differentiation processes, simultaneous trajectory inference and gene regulatory network reconstruction remain challenging. We propose bowside, a shallow neural stochastic differentiation model that mechanistically models gene regulation. Our method successfully recovers gene expression trends and the underlying regulatory interactions. We demonstrate bowside on hematopoiesis and induced pluripotent stem cell reprogramming data, retrieving known fate-determining network motifs.

last_author.name: Claassen, M.
last_author.affiliation: University Hospital Tübingen

preprints.title: Molecule-resolved inference reveals the spatial organization of transcriptional programs
preprints.abstract: Transcriptional programs encode cellular identity and physiological activity, linking gene regulation to cellular phenotypes. Although spatial transcriptomics measures individual RNA molecules across intact tissues, most analyses aggregate them into cells or pixels, obscuring molecular level functional dynamics. We introduce FICTURE2, a statistical model that infers the transcriptional program from which each individual molecule is generated, using gene identity and spatial context alone without segmentation or binning. FICTURE2 learns programs with distinct spatial distributions, ranging from millimeter-scale continuous transition to micron-scale subcellular localization, the coexisting patterns of which then reveal both cellular identity and physiological activity with unified interpretations. FICTURE2 supports both unsupervised and reference-guided inference and is orders of magnitude more efficient than alternative approaches, enabling systematic analysis of large-scale spatial datasets as we demonstrate in data across diverse tissue types profiled by various spatial technologies.

preprints.title: Organ scale Three-dimensional atlas of developing pelvic innervation for the mouse lower urinary tract.
preprints.abstract: Pelvic autonomic neurons are responsible for coordinating pelvic organ function, including storage and emptying of the urinary bladder. These neurons arise from sacral neural crest-derived progenitors which migrate to the developing urogenital sinus and undergo differentiation alongside pelvic organs, ultimately organizing into paired pelvic ganglia. To circumvent the complex morphological changes that occur during genitourinary organ development, we have optimized light sheet fluorescence microscopy imaging for three-dimensional mapping of the development and spatial distribution of pelvic autonomic neurons. To track neural crest progenitor migration, neurogenesis, and formation of mature pelvic ganglia morphology in mice, we imaged intact lower urinary tract tissue from mid-gestational to post-weaning stages at single-cell resolution. The resulting atlas identifies the precise timing and initial routes of neural crest progenitor migration, defines timing for pelvic ganglion neurogenesis, and reveals previously unrecognized neuronal cell bodies outside of the centralized pelvic ganglia structures. The analysis further highlights morphological changes to pelvic ganglion structure that occur in parallel with genitourinary maturation, including the divergence of the major pelvic ganglia and bladder-proximal accessory ganglia. This work acts as the first wholemount imaging atlas of pelvic innervation in the mouse spanning fetal and postnatal timepoints, and thus we present an informative tool for future studies of developmental neurourology and neurogenic bladder dysfunction.

preprints.title: Pycea: a scverse toolkit for single-cell lineage tracing analysis
preprints.abstract: Lineage tracing enables reconstruction of cellular histories in development, regeneration, and disease, but integrating lineage data into single-cell analysis workflows remains challenging. We introduce Pycea, a Python toolkit for lineage analysis and visualization, and TreeData, an extension of AnnData that stores lineage trees alongside cellular measurements. TreeData is compatible with Scanpy and other scverse tools, enabling integrated analysis without converting between formats. Pycea provides scalable methods for tree visualization, clade identification, distance comparisons, ancestral state inference, and lineage statistics. This software is open source and available at https://github.com/YosefLab/pycea.

preprints.title: Regionalisation of muscle nucleus heterogeneity in foetal skeletal muscle
preprints.abstract: Skeletal muscle is organized into functional domains with attachments at both extremities to tendons via the myotendinous junction (MTJ) and innervation in the middle via the neuromuscular junction (NMJ). In adult muscle, the molecular heterogeneity of muscle domains is described at the level of myonuclei with specialized MTJ and NMJ myonuclei at the tips and middle of muscle fibre. However, how molecular heterogeneity emerges during development remains poorly understood. Combining single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing approaches with in situ hybridization experiments to limb muscles of chicken embryos, we uncover transcriptionally distinct muscle nuclei according to tip and central domains, both in myofibres and in mononucleated myogenic cells. At early foetal stage, all myonuclei display either a tip or a central domain identity. Immature mononucleated myogenic cells are enriched in the tip domain. Tip myonuclei of foetal muscles show a robust transcriptional signal transduction signature, which highlights molecular crosstalks between tip myonuclei and adjacent tendon fibroblasts but also with the adjacent immature mononucleated myogenic cells. We propose that the tip muscle domain is a signalling centre interacting with tendon fibroblasts to regulate muscle/tendon attachment and with adjacent mononucleated muscle cells to regulate myogenesis in limb foetal muscles.

preprints.title: Unsupervised prioritization of gene-regulatory variants with isolation forests
preprints.abstract: Most common variants occur in non-coding genomic regions. Numerous expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) can influence nearby gene expression. Across diverse traits and diseases, many genome-wide association study (GWAS) loci have been shown to colocalize with eQTLs, supporting gene-regulatory causal mechanisms. However, linkage disequilibrium (LD) obscures the identification of the causal variant(s), necessitating prioritization by functional annotations. Previously published variant prioritization tools relied on the machine-learning-based combination of diverse feature types like evolutionary conservation and chromatin information, whereas more recent deep learning tools learn and describe gene-regulatory DNA sequence grammar. However, the latter approaches often generate a large number of scores per variant. We designed a novel unsupervised machine-learning approach based on isolation forests to integrate the predictions from the broadly used Enformer deep learning model into a single gene-regulatory predictive score for each common variant. Our novel approach eQTL prediction with isolation forests (eQIF) demonstrates strong performance in predicting eQTLs and gene-regulatory GWAS variants. We show that top eQIF variants are located in evolutionarily conserved transcription factor binding site (TFBS) footprints, and that the frequency of top eQIF variants within overrepresented TFBS motifs recapitulates the motif information content. eQIF predictions are precomputed for 9,431,969 common variants and publicly available.

preprints.title: scRM: A single-cell foundation model trained on scRNA-seq reads
preprints.abstract: To our knowledge, scRM is the first single-cell foundation model trained on sequencing reads, demonstrating that raw data pretraining is not only feasible but competitive at a fraction of the computational cost. We anticipate that scaling this framework and exploring alternative architectures will unlock biological information inaccessible to count models and extend the dataset-specific pretraining it already makes possible. The source code is available at https://github.com/altoslabs/scRM.

preprints.title: A conserved Foxp1-Pde4d axis regulates inflammatory responsiveness
preprints.abstract: Inflammatory responses are heterogeneous, even among cells exposed to a common insult, yet the regulatory mechanisms that distinguish these inflammatory states remain poorly understood. Here, we leveraged inflammatory state heterogeneity to identify a conserved Foxp1-Pde4d regulatory relationship and uncover a role for this axis in preserving inflammatory responsiveness. Genotoxic stress in adipocyte progenitors generated heterogeneous engagement of type-I interferon (IFN) and NF{kappa}B transcriptional programmes, and transcriptome-wide analysis independently identified Foxp1 and the cAMP phosphodiesterase Pde4d among genes associated with lower IFN- and higher NF{kappa}B-associated transcription. ChIP-seq revealed selective loss of Foxp1 occupancy at a Pde4d-associated regulatory element following genotoxic stress, while Foxp1 gain- and loss-of-function established Foxp1 as a positive regulator of Pde4d expression. Remarkably, coupling of Foxp1-Pde4d expression was broadly conserved across vertebrate tissues and damage models. In vivo, Foxp1 loss in zebrafish revealed a striking dissociation between inflammatory state and response capacity: basal NF{kappa}B activity was elevated, yet injury-induced NF{kappa}B activation was markedly blunted and macrophage recruitment impaired. Adenylyl cyclase inhibition restored macrophage recruitment in Foxp1-deficient zebrafish, functionally linking the Foxp1 phenotype to cAMP signalling and supporting a model in which Foxp1-Pde4d regulation preserves inflammatory responsiveness through control of cAMP. Together, these findings show how inflammatory-state heterogeneity can reveal conserved regulatory mechanisms linking basal cellular state to subsequent response capacity.

preprints.title: A network of bZIP transcription factors and inhibitors enforces differentially proliferative and cytotoxic states in T cells
preprints.abstract: The bZIP family of transcription factors (TFs) plays a central role in regulating T-cell exhaustion. Their complex dimeric interactions obscure the roles of individual members, which genetic knockout or overexpression alone poorly resolve. Here, we use overexpression of full-length bZIP family TFs alongside genetically encoded, protein-based inhibitors to probe the effect of increased or decreased bZIP TF activity on CAR T-cell expansion under exhausting conditions. Enrichment of inhibitors of pro-exhaustion TFs (CREM, NFIL3) illustrated the utility of this approach. The screen enriched full-length TFs of established anti-exhaustion relevance and identified underappreciated bZIP TFs such as BATF2. Detailed comparison of several bZIP TFs and inhibitors revealed distinct effects on proliferation, persistence, and cytotoxicity. We investigated combinations of pro-cytotoxic JUN, pro-proliferative BATF2, and a novel inhibitor (AEL-CREM) of pro-dysfunction CREM. Distinct pairs were more advantageous for maintenance of cytotoxicity or proliferation, revealing relationships between BATF2, JUN-, and CREB1-family bZIPs. Using a combination of epistasis, transcriptome, proteome, and AP-MS interactome analyses of BATF2 and AEL-CREM, we discovered functional overlap in their inhibition of pro-dysfunction CREB1-family activity, potentially driven by unexpected binding of CREB1-family members by overexpressed BATF2. Their function diverged in BATF2's early promotion of pro-proliferation AP-1 activity and later physical and functional interactions with BACH2, contributing to persistence. These findings were mirrored in murine chronic viral infection and syngeneic tumor models, where BATF2 or AEL-CREM overexpression were notably pro-proliferative and anti-exhaustion. Together, these results illuminate new connections and functional roles enabled by bZIP family perturbations, with implications for modulating T-cell state.

preprints.title: Aging reshapes cardiac extravascular leukocyte transcription through bidirectional remodeling during LPS-induced endotoxemia
preprints.abstract: Sepsis disproportionately affects older adults and is frequently complicated by cardiac dysfunction. However, how aging alters the transcriptional responses of cardiac extravascular immune cells during systemic inflammation remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated aging-dependent transcriptional remodeling of cardiac immune cells using an LPS-induced endotoxemia model in young and aged C57BL/6 mice. Mice received intraperitoneal LPS (5 mg/kg body weight) or vehicle, and cardiac extravascular leukocytes were isolated from ex vivo retrogradely perfused hearts 24 h later for single-cell RNA sequencing. Aging was associated with bidirectional transcriptional remodeling, characterized by both up- and downregulation of gene programs, particularly in cardiac macrophages, monocyte-like macrophages, T cells, and B cells following LPS challenge. A shared feature across these four cell populations was reduced representation of mitochondrial-associated transcriptional programs, indicating aging-dependent remodeling of mitochondrial biology across cardiac myeloid and lymphoid lineages during systemic inflammation. In parallel, cell type-specific transcriptional remodeling revealed distinct functional-associated responses. Macrophages and monocyte-like macrophages exhibited increased tissue-remodeling and repair-associated transcriptional programs. Both T and B cells showed reduced metabolic programs but increased actin cytoskeleton organization. T cells additionally exhibited reduced cytotoxicity-associated and enhanced Th17-associated transcriptional programs, whereas B cells showed reduced antigen-processing and presentation programs. Cell-cell communication analysis suggested aging-associated differences in immune cell interactions following LPS challenge and potential features of cardiac inflammaging at baseline. Together, these findings demonstrate that aging bidirectionally reshapes the cardiac immune response to systemic inflammation, characterized by shared remodeling of mitochondrial-associated programs and cell type-specific changes in inflammatory, metabolic, cytoskeletal, and effector-associated programs. These aging-dependent transcriptional changes occurred in the context of the greater severity of illness observed in aged mice following LPS-induced endotoxemia.

preprints.title: An Ovol1 Variant in Endothelial Cells Regulates Slug and is Essential for Pathological Angiogenesis
preprints.abstract: During development, the blood vasculature expands by sprouting angiogenesis, but the programs that guide this process can become dysregulated in the pathological angiogenesis of neovascular diseases leading to excessive disorganized blood vessels. We previously reported that in endothelial cells, the pro-mesenchymal transcription factor Slug critically regulates angiogenesis through a partial and reversible endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (pEndoMT); however, the upstream regulators that activate Slug and may contribute to pathological activation of the pEndoMT pathway in disease are still poorly understood. Here, we show that endothelial cells express an unusual low molecular weight variant of Ovol1 - a zinc-finger transcription factor that regulates mesenchymal transition in epithelial cells. Ovol1 and Slug are co-expressed in angiogenic endothelial cells, and using ChIP, we confirm direct Ovol1 binding to the endogenous Slug gene at a species-conserved binding motif. Whereas Ovol1 is typically a transcriptional repressor in epithelial cells, we find using a combination of silencing RNA and lentiviral overexpression constructs that the endothelial Ovol1 variant upregulates Slug, and is sufficient to drive pEndoMT marker expression and enhance endothelial cell migratory capacity. Silencing of Ovol1 abolished sprouting angiogenesis in a 3D in vitro sprouting angiogenesis assay, whereas constitutive overexpression of Ovol1 produced overaggressive and disorganized hypersprouting that depends upon Slug. We generated Ovol1 or Slug endothelial-specific knockout mice (Ovol1ECKO and SlugECKO) and found that healthy developmental angiogenesis of the neonatal mouse retina proceeds relatively normally in knockout animals. By contrast, Ovol1 was reduced in established post-natal blood vessels but became strongly re-expressed in tumor endothelial cells, and we found that colorectal cancer syngraft growth was significantly reduced in both Ovol1ECKO and SlugECKO mice alongside a failure of tumor angiogenesis. Lastly, neovascularization in the oxygen-induced retinopathy (OIR) model was also reduced in SlugECKO mice. In conclusion, we report that an endothelial Ovol1 variant upregulates Slug and drives a mesenchymal-like state, and that this Ovol1-Slug pEndoMT signaling axis is essential for pathological angiogenesis in neovascular disease models.

preprints.title: Anatomically matched spatial comparisons identify Trps1 as a regulator of knee interzone formation
preprints.abstract: How the interzone forms and gives rise to articular cartilage, ligaments, and synovium is incompletely understood. Using our previously generated spatial and single-cell transcriptomic atlas of the mouse hindlimb, we compared the knee interzone with neighboring tissues and with the ankle interzone at matched positions, and identified Trps1 as a knee interzone-enriched candidate. Pseudotime analysis placed Trps1-high cells in a transitional state between chondrogenic progenitors and matrix-producing chondrocytes, with higher chondrogenic and lower fibroblastic program scores. Targeted Trps1 knockdown in hindlimb explants disrupted joint formation, permitted Col2a1 expression within the interzone, and reduced adjacent cartilage formation. The associated chondrogenic program was conserved in the human embryonic knee, whereas TRPS1 expression in osteoarthritic cartilage was associated with a fibroblastic matrix program. These results support a role for Trps1 in knee interzone development and show that anatomically matched spatial comparison with explant perturbation can nominate and test joint regulators.

preprints.title: CD200R1 Marks a Branchpoint During Human Natural Killer Cell Development in Tonsils
preprints.abstract: Human natural killer (NK) cells arise from common innate lymphoid cell (ILC) progenitor and precursor populations that are selectively enriched within secondary lymphoid tissues (SLTs) and that complete their terminal differentiation through stages of progressively lineage-restricted downstream developmental intermediates. We identify two subsets of tonsil CD94/NKG2A+NKp80- (stage 4A) NK-cell development intermediates that show differential expression of the inhibitory receptor, CD200R1. Ex vivo single-cell transcriptomic, DNA methylation, phenotypic, and functional analyses demonstrate that CD200R1 stage 4A cells represent an immature, oligopotent precursor population enriched for tissue-resident and cytokine-responsive programs. In contrast, CD200R1- stage 4A cells show more restricted NK-cell developmental potential concomitant with features of mature NK cells. These findings help to refine the human NK cell developmental pathway in tonsils and highlight CD200R1 as a useful marker delineating an uncommitted developmental state linking microenvironmental cues to NK-cell maturation and plasticity.

preprints.title: Carrier-Limited Release Risk in Electrospun Nanofibers for Regenerative Endodontics: Constraint Discovery from 25 Formulations
preprints.abstract: Regenerative endodontics needs an intracanal carrier that keeps disinfecting across a dressing interval that clinicians schedule at one to four weeks, without harming the stem cells that rebuild the pulp. We ask what one completed 25-formulation electrospinning campaign of poly(vinylpyrrolidone) (PVP) fibers carrying metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, minocycline and Ca(OH)2 can decide, and use machine learning for constraint discovery and decision support rather than as a new predictor. After an audit against the source thesis, logistic regression predicts fine-fiber formation at 96% leave-one-out accuracy, but a one-threshold rule does as well, the gain over the 80% majority baseline is not significant (exact McNemar p = 0.125), and accuracy falls to 84% when mixture loading is encoded per component. Diameter models interpolate within formulation families (ridge MAE 193 nm, 95% CI 96 to 317 nm) and fail across them (R^2 < 0). Because the campaign never measured release, we assemble a same-drug, cross-carrier evidence table: 17 bounded metronidazole and ciprofloxacin observations from seven studies, with two-sided censoring. Water-soluble carriers (PVP, PVA) completed release within 80 h (PVP within 8 h); no water-insoluble monolithic carrier reached 90% within its observation window, releasing 1.5 to 50%; both within-study comparisons separate at matched loading; and blend, core-shell and thick-mat architectures released over 3 to 28 days. The PVP mats therefore carry a carrier-limited release risk, not a proven ceiling, and one dissolution experiment can confirm or overturn it. A censoring-aware screen keeps three necessarily and one possibly nondominated formulation, and fixed-budget replays show that uncertainty sampling finds failed formulations sooner, except the one it is confidently wrong about.

preprints.title: Caudate nucleus aging and its association with brain disorders
preprints.abstract: The caudate nucleus supports cognition and goal-directed behavior, undergoes age-associated changes, and is implicated in substance use, psychiatric, and neurodegenerative disorders. However, how aging alters its diverse cell types and how such changes relate to diseases remains poorly understood. To address these questions, we assembled single nucleus transcriptomic atlases of the caudate tissue, comprising 963,842 nuclei from 178 human donors, including controls and individuals with alcohol use disorder (AUD) or opioid use disorder (OUD), and 83,699 nuclei from six healthy rhesus macaques. We also curated 3,139 bulk RNA-seq profiles from the caudate and other brain regions spanning controls and multiple diagnostic groups, as well as paired RNA and chromatin accessibility profiles from 257,524 caudate nuclei across 161 control and AUD donors. These datasets enabled comparisons across age, species, brain regions, and diagnostic groups. We found shared glial aging features in humans and macaques, whereas neuronal changes were more divergent. Inferred neuron-to-neuron communication declined with age, with greater declines in AUD. Both transcriptional and chromatin accessibility profiles showed nonlinear age-associated patterns, with pronounced changes in later adulthood. In donors with AUD, age-associated changes appeared earlier, with altered trajectories in lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function, and neuronal signaling. Across comparisons involving AUD, OUD, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and Alzheimer disease, mitochondrial function and fatty acid metabolism emerged as consensus features linking caudate aging to diseases, although the direction and extent of overlap varied by disorder and brain region. Together, these findings define cellular and regulatory features of primate caudate aging and reveal shared and context-dependent relationships between aging and brain disorders.

preprints.title: Defining cell type-specific diurnal gene expression in the mouse retina
preprints.abstract: The mammalian retina exhibits daily oscillations in gene expression that contribute to retinal physiology and visual function. However, the extent to which these temporal patterns differ among retinal cell types remains incompletely understood. We performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing in the mouse retina over the day and night, identifying rhythmic genes in the six major retinal cell types. Distinct diurnal gene expression patterns across photoreceptors, interneurons, retinal ganglion cells, and Muller glia correspond to their diverse functions across the light cycle. Even core circadian clock genes exhibited differences in paralog expression and rhythmicity across the retina. In contrast, dopamine signaling via the DRD4 receptor is highly rhythmic across most retinal cell types, suggesting dopamine signaling may be a key rhythmicity cue in the retina under diurnal conditions. This dataset highlights the complexity of daily transcriptional regulation in the retina and provides a resource to explore cell-type-specific diurnal rhythms.

preprints.title: Dissecting the genetic basis of DUS characters in Pakistani wheat varieties
preprints.abstract: Distinctness, Uniformity and Stability (DUS) testing is fundamental to varietal characterization and the protection of Plant Breeders Rights (PBRs), but conventional DUS assessment relies predominantly on morphological characteristics whose expression may be influenced by environmental conditions, developmental stage and observer-related variation. Integrating character-specific molecular markers with conventional DUS assessment may therefore improve the reproducibility and genetic resolution of varietal identification. This study investigated the genetic architecture of DUS characteristics in a panel of 102 historical and modern Pakistani wheat varieties using genome-wide association studies (GWAS). Phenotypic variation was evaluated using distribution, correlation and hierarchical clustering analyses, while the germplasm was genotyped using a wheat genotyping-by-targeted sequencing platform. After quality filtering, 21,670 high-quality single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were retained for analyses of genetic diversity, population structure, linkage disequilibrium (LD) and marker-trait associations. Population structure analysis indicated extensive admixture, with cross-entropy supporting K = 9 ancestral components, whereas hierarchical genetic clustering separated the germplasm into five broad groups. The first three principal components explained 8.09%, 7.20% and 5.39% of the total genetic variation, respectively. GWAS using BLINK and FarmCPU identified significant associations for several diagnostically important DUS characteristics. Growth habit was strongly associated with SNP 1B_129176704, with an additional signal on chromosome 5B. Shattering showed its strongest association at 1D_445256324, accompanied by several closely linked SNPs in the same region and a secondary significant locus at 7B_703502819. Flag leaf length was associated with a cluster of SNPs on chromosome 6A, while tiller density showed a major association with 5D_205488820. These findings demonstrate substantial phenotypic and genetic diversity within Pakistani wheat germplasm and identify genomic regions that merit validation as character-specific molecular tools to complement conventional DUS testing and PBR implementation.

preprints.title: EMBER: Contextualized gene representations enable compositional prediction across cellular perturbations
preprints.abstract: Predicting the effects of individual and combined perturbations is central to identifying context-specific vulnerabilities and designing targeted interventions. Yet learning gene representations that integrate functional relationships with cellular state and transfer across perturbation tasks remains challenging. Here, we present EMBER, a gene-centric foundation model that learns context-dependent functional representations of genes. EMBER combines interaction-guided contrastive learning with masked expression reconstruction during pretraining on a single-cell corpus curated for diversity and balanced sampling across cell types and experimental batches. EMBER decouples gene representation learning from task-specific prediction through a composable embedding framework: the pretrained encoder remains frozen, while lightweight probes combine contextualized gene embeddings to predict individual and combined perturbation effects. The same pretrained representations support single-gene perturbation-response prediction, digenic interaction prediction, and multi-target drug-response prediction. EMBER improves cross-context perturbation-response prediction and genetic-interaction ranking relative to evaluated baselines. EMBER also prioritized SCFD1, a mediator of autophagosome-lysosome fusion, as a candidate dependency during mTOR inhibition. Together, these results establish contextualized gene embeddings as reusable building blocks for modeling genetic and pharmacological perturbations, supporting the prioritization of genetic interactions and context-specific interventions for experimental testing.

preprints.title: Early Progression Cells mark a stem-like state associated with pancreatic cancer initiation and progression
preprints.abstract: Pancreatic cancer is deemed to progress from microscopic pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanINs). However, low grade PanINs are frequently detected in the general population without presentation or increased risk of developing cancer, suggesting that many PanINs never progress to tumours. What precisely characterises PanINs that develop into tumours is insufficiently understood. Using a mouse model where pancreatitis-induced tissue injury promotes pancreatic cancer from rare KrasG12D cells, we identify Early Progression Cells (EPCs) as a new entity, a novel population of cancer stem-like cells. Transcriptomic analyses illustrate EPCs as stress-adapted, inflammation responsive stem cells that also upregulate gene programmes indicative of microenvironment remodelling. Using identified EPC protein markers, we show that EPCs are prevalent in early metaplastic stages and in PanIN progression from low grade to high grade but are rarer in tumours. PanIN- and tumour-derived sphere and organoid assays demonstrate that EPCs possess all characteristics of stem cells in vitro and are dependent on Nupr1 stress response pathways for survival and growth. We identify APP-CD74 as a novel cell-cell interaction pathway between EPCs and neighbouring epithelial cells in PanINs and tumours. Inhibition of CD74 activity in vitro induces high-grade PanIN organoid death, suggesting EPCs are critical for high-grade PanINs. Using spatial transcriptomics of human samples, we detect gene signatures of EPCs in distinct regions of human PanIN and PDAC tissues, including APP-CD74 interactions, providing compelling evidence that EPCs are relevant to human disease. Further understanding of EPC biology will likely uncover new knowledge on why rare PanINs progress towards tumours.

preprints.title: Epigenetic reprogramming by promoter hypomethylation is linked to aberrant gene expression and transcriptomic plasticity in colorectal cancer
preprints.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) has high phenotypic plasticity, but regulatory mechanisms of aberrant cell states are not well described. We investigated DNA methylation-based regulation of cancer cell-intrinsic transcriptomic heterogeneity in 1,183 multiregional primary tumor samples, liver metastases and tumor organoids. Most genes with strong methylation-transcriptomic association reflected canonical promoter hypermethylation and expression repression related to the CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP). However, promoter hypomethylation and overexpression of APOLD1 and ELF5 identified two largely non-overlapping subgroups of canonical CIMP-negative CRCs enriched with stem-like and transit-amplifying cell states. APOLD1 tumors were further highly proliferative while ELF5 tumors were slow-cycling and associated with good survival in early-stage disease. Target genes showed patient-specific expression changes in matched primary-metastasis samples, and ELF5 aberrant metastases showed ex vivo sensitivity to putative targeting of stem cells by PI3K/mTOR inhibition, fetal de-differentiation and transition into non-canonical intestinal states. This implicates focal promoter hypomethylation in phenotypic plasticity in CRC metastasis.

preprints.title: Evolutionary conservation and divergence of regional fructose-responsive gene regulation in the intestine
preprints.abstract: Sugar-responsive gene regulation in peripheral organs facilitates safe utilization of fructose. Intestine is the first-line site for fructose catabolism, converting fructose into less harmful metabolites. Its metabolism is spatially organized along the proximodistal axis, but how intestinal zonation shapes responses to fructose and to what extent these responses are evolutionarily conserved remain poorly understood. Here, we examine regional gene regulation in response to acute fructose challenge across the small intestine of mouse and Drosophila. Fructose exposure elicited both ubiquitous and regionally biased regulation of metabolic genes. Unlike prolonged feeding on a complex high-carbohydrate diet, fructose feeding activated the heat shock and immune responses, with proximal and distal biases, respectively. The ChREBP/Mondo-Mlx pathway emerged as the major regulator of fructose-responsive gene expression, with a conserved role in regulation of both ubiquitous and region-restricted metabolic targets. Comparative analysis of orthologous genes revealed conserved activation of glucose metabolism, nutrient transport, and stress-responsive pathways, but also notable divergence in downstream metabolic programs. Whereas mouse intestine activates pathways required for fructose conversion into glucose, Drosophila preferentially activates de novo lipogenesis. Thus, intestinal gene regulation provides a conserved protective mechanism against high fructose challenge, but the pathways involved have partially diverged during evolution.

preprints.title: Full-Term and Preterm Differences in Human Brain Functional Connectivity Development Across Birth
preprints.abstract: We possess a limited understanding of how preterm and full-term brains develop during the earliest stages of life, from the fetal to neonatal period, and how they respond to the birth transition. Here, we characterize brain resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) using over 1000 longitudinal fetal and infant functional MRI scans from 21 to 52 post-conception weeks across birth. By mapping the developmental trajectory of RSFC across this window, we unveil marked divergences in developmental patterns between preterm- and term-born brains at both the global and network levels. When aligned by birth, the full-term group exhibit generally higher RSFC than the preterm group. For selected between-network connections with a significant prematurity effect, full-term cases demonstrate an overall increase in RSFC across age, whereas preterm cases show minimal change or even a decrease in connectivity of these systems. In contrast, when aligned by postconceptional age, the preterm group shows an accelerated increase in RSFC between 30 and 40 weeks. Across comparisons, mode of delivery and sex showed minimal influence on these trajectories. These findings offer novel insight into how prematurity and early exposure to the extrauterine environment alter the developmental trajectories of large-scale neural networks, advancing our understanding of both typical and preterm brain development.

preprints.title: Functional Mammary Gland Organoids From Human Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells
preprints.abstract: The human mammary gland arises through sequential lineage restrictions from surface ectoderm to hormone-responsive bilayered epithelium, yet a tractable in vitro model that captures these events has remained elusive. Here, we established a stepwise differentiation protocol that directs human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) into mammary organoids (MGOs) by sequential induction of non-neural ectoderm, mammary placodes, and lineage maturation in a defined medium. The resulting MGOs reproducibly formed polarized basal (KRT14+, TP63+) and luminal (KRT8+, GATA3+) layers, with ~25% of luminal cells expressing oestrogen receptor (ER). MGOs accumulated lipids, expressed {beta}-casein upon prolactin stimulation, and retained lineage fidelity after serial passaging. Upon transplantation into cleared mouse mammary fat pads, MGOs generated branched mammary ductal networks. Single-cell transcriptomics confirmed the emergence of basal, luminal hormone-sensing, luminal secretory, and stromal populations, transcriptionally aligned with adult human breast epithelium and responsive to endocrine disruption. These findings demonstrate that hiPSCs can be reprogrammed into functional mammary epithelium, providing a platform to dissect development, endocrine signalling, and breast cancer pathogenesis.

last_author.name: van de Water, B.
last_author.affiliation: Leiden University

preprints.title: GPBench: A benchmark framework for genomic prediction
preprints.abstract: Genomic prediction (GP) has emerged as a powerful data mining strategy for disease risk assessment and molecular breeding. GP leverages genome-wide genetic variations and phenotypic information through a computational model to estimate genetic potential or disease risk. However, the field of GP still faces several major challenges: (i) dataset bias and insufficient representativeness; (ii) the lack of standardized evaluation protocols and a systematic benchmarking framework; (iii) heavy reliance on empirical expertise for experimental result interpretation, which hinders large-scale and systematic analysis. These issues make it difficult to conduct systematic cross-species evaluation and comparison of GP methods, and their authentic applications. To address these challenges, we established a standardized and extensible GP benchmark framework-GPBench. We first collected and harmonized public datasets from 16 species, covering animals, plants, and microorganisms, comprising 57 traits, 40,821 samples, and 493,821 single-nucleotide polymorphisms. Then, using the standardized datasets, the framework evaluates 21 GP models and provides a unified assessment across four dimensions: effectiveness, sensitivity, robustness, and scalability. Furthermore, we developed a large language model-based intelligent analysis system to facilitate the interpretation of GP experiments and model recommendations. GPBench provides the community with a fair, unified, and scalable platform (https://www.sdu-idea.cn/GPBench/) and an open-source library for comparing and optimizing GP methods, ultimately accelerating the application of GP in life sciences and biomedical research.

preprints.title: Local chromatin, 3D genome folding and transposon cargo shape Sleeping Beauty transposition
preprints.abstract: The cut-and-paste DNA transposon Sleeping Beauty (SB) is widely used for genome engineering, mutagenesis and gene delivery. When mobilized from a genomic donor position ("launch site"), SB preferentially reintegrates locally (< 2 Mb), but factors governing its transposition from genomic sites remain incompletely understood. Here we analysed local transposition experiments in mouse embryonic stem cells to determine the influence of chromatin context and transposon cargo on SB transposition. Transposons in launch sites with transcriptionally active, accessible chromatin showed lower transposition efficiency. Large cargo and cargo with higher transcriptional activity also result in reduced transposition efficiency. After excision, local reintegration patterns closely resembled 3D contact frequencies of the launch site. This indicates that chromosome folding is a major determinant of the transposition pattern. Surprisingly, we did not detect any effect of the destination chromatin composition on reintegration efficiency. Cargo sequence modified the reintegration patterns: promoter-containing cargo increased both very proximal (<10kb) and interchromosomal transpositions, while CTCF binding sites in the cargo increased reintegration on the launch chromosome. Together, these results define key determinants of SB transposition in chromosomes and inform the design of SB-based genome engineering strategies.

preprints.title: Mixing, competence, and commitment set the stability of cell identity
preprints.abstract: Cells maintain their identities in the face of molecular noise, yet can change them rapidly when cued. Here, we treat this tension as a problem in the control of a stochastic system. We represent a cell identity as a set of molecular configurations, or microstates, among which cells undergo stochastic transitions, and measure its stability by the effective rate of commitment to another identity, using a Markov model in which committed cells are removed. Mixing, competence, and commitment provide three channels for tuning this rate. They govern microstate transitions, how commitment is distributed among microstates, and the overall speed of commitment, respectively. Control over the effective commitment rate is shared between commitment and mixing in proportions that always sum to one. Interventions with the same effective commitment rate cannot be told apart by survival alone but, given the microstate transition rates, can be distinguished by the fraction of cells in each microstate or by how quickly cells sorted on permissive microstates commit. When competence varies in time, pulsed commitment signalling commits more cells than sustained signalling of equal dose, by an amount that grows with the depth of that variation, whereas with constant competence pulsing gains nothing in the models we studied. This suggests a possible function for pulsatile signalling, such as that of ERK, which the experiments we propose could test. Finally, reanalysing single-cell imaging of mouse embryonic stem cells leaving naive pluripotency, we estimate that cells take about as long to acquire competence as they then wait to commit, and we specify experiments to identify which channel drives this exit.

preprints.title: Multimodal profiling and intersectional genetics reveal CA1 border inhibitory neuron diversity and postnatal emergence of retrosplenial connectivity
preprints.abstract: Inhibitory neurons (INs) at the stratum radiatum/stratum lacunosum-moleculare border of hippocampal CA1 comprise diverse populations, including long-range-projecting neurons that innervate the retrosplenial cortex (RSCtx). However, their molecular organization and developmental connectivity remain poorly understood. Here, we combine multimodal transcriptomic profiling, intersectional genetics, and retrograde tracing to characterize CA1 border INs. We identified two major caudal ganglionic eminence-derived, Cxcl14-enriched populations distinguished by Syt6/Cck-related and Ntng1-expressing transcriptional profiles. We then generated a Cxcl14-Cre mouse line that, when combined with an IN-specific viral enhancer, provides genetic access to CA1 border INs. Retrograde labeling established that CA1 INs projecting to the RSCtx belong to the Ntng1-expressing population, and that this long-range projection emerges during postnatal mouse development, between postnatal days 3 and 5. Finally, analysis of genes encoding cell-surface proteins, key regulators of connectivity, revealed distinct expression profiles in RSCtx-projecting and SYT6-positive INs. Together, these findings establish a molecular and developmental framework for CA1 border IN diversity and provide a genetic strategy for investigating the assembly and function of these inhibitory circuits.

last_author.name: De Wit, J.
last_author.affiliation: VIB-KU Leuven Center for Neuroscience

preprints.title: NEPTUNE: a neuronal cell death pathway prediction tool used to decipher neurodegeneration using single cell RNA-seq datasets
preprints.abstract: In the constantly evolving landscape of cell death mechanisms, much of the literature is dominated by research performed in cancer cells and regenerating cell types. However, neurons differ in that they are non-regenerating and post-mitotic. Therefore, assessing neuronal specific disease biomarkers, including cell death markers, without the bias of non-neuronal or cancerous cells, could provide a more biologically accurate neurodegeneration profile. In this study, we developed the Neuronal cEll death Prediction Tool for Understanding Neurodegenerative Events (NEPTUNE), a user-friendly tool for researchers that bioinformatically identifies neuronal cell death markers from user provided differentially expressed gene lists obtained by single cell RNA sequencing data. We applied NEPTUNE to a publicly available single cell RNA sequencing dataset and analysed the progression of photoreceptor degeneration in the rd1 mouse model of severe retinitis pigmentosa. The analysis interpreted the dataset in a neuronal-specific manner and showed that late-stage photoreceptor death is not purely apoptotic but possibly engages overlapping cell death programmes. From the analysis, the user is provided with publishable graphs and a list of cell death markers with fold change, type of impact, cell death type and a strength score. Overall, our tool provides markers specific to neurodegeneration, allows mapping to known WikiPathways and KEGG pathways, performs GO and KEGG enrichment analysis and plots the data for further analysis, greatly facilitating the study of neuron specific degeneration. The tool can be found at: https://neptune.rgtcarvalholab.com/.

last_author.name: Carvalho, L. S.
last_author.affiliation: University of Melbourne

preprints.title: OncoSpot enables benchmarking of cancer spatial transcriptomics methods across tumor evolutionary modes
preprints.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) is increasingly used to map clonal architecture within tumors, yet methods for analyzing cancer ST data are difficult to evaluate because real tumors lack ground truth for copy-number alterations (CNAs), subclonal identity, and malignant cell fraction. Existing ST simulators model normal tissue and do not represent tumor evolution, CNA-driven expression, or the spatial organization of malignant subclones. We present OncoSpot, a cancer-aware simulator of Visium-like spot-based ST data. OncoSpot combines a spatial evolutionary scaffold from DEMON, CNAs generated along the resulting clonal phylogeny with CNAsim, cancer-type-specific malignant transcriptional programs, and spatially clustered nonmalignant cell types, and aggregates cells into spots with known malignant fraction, subclone, and copy-number profiles. We demonstrate OncoSpot on high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, colorectal cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma, which represent three distinct modes of tumor evolution. Simulated subclones were spatially clustered and showed stronger phylogeny-space concordance than those generated by scCube under matched subclone populations. Benchmarking CopyKAT, CancerFinder, Clonalscope, and RCTD revealed cancer-dependent performance: Clonalscope recovered copy-number signals more accurately in ovarian and colorectal cancer, whereas CopyKAT performed better in hepatocellular carcinoma, reflecting both the assumptions of each method and the copy-number landscapes of the three cancers. OncoSpot's ground truth also exposed a failure mode in Clonalscope's malignant spot identification, in which tumor and normal labels were inverted, and allowed us to trace its cause. These method-dependent behaviors would be difficult to detect in real data. OncoSpot provides a framework for benchmarking CNA inference, subclone detection, malignant spot identification, and normal spot deconvolution, and its modular design and guidelines allow extension to additional cancer types. OncoSpot is freely available at https://github.com/compbio-mallory/OncoSpot.

last_author.name: Mallory, X.
last_author.affiliation: Florida State University

preprints.title: PPI-Rescue: restoration of eye development via functional reconstitution of a transcription complex.
preprints.abstract: The activity of transcription factors (TFs) can be modulated through protein-protein interactions (PPIs) with cofactors which can serve to enhance, repress or alter the specificity of TF function. Current genetic and molecular approaches such as knockout and overexpression studies are likely to affect all possible activities of a TF, presenting a dilemma when attempting to parse out how TFs function within a cell. Hence, there is a need to devise a technique that will allow for mechanistic insight to be gained into the function(s) of discrete transcription complexes. Herein we report ''PPI-Rescue'', an approach that leverages bespoke mutations in TFs and the selective reconstitution of specific complexes to study the molecular properties and biological functions of discrete transcription complexes in vitro and in vivo. We demonstrate PPI-Rescue using the conserved Drosophila transcription factor Sine oculis (So) and cofactor Eyes Absent (Eya). To validate this approach, we engineered a missense mutation, So{Delta}Eya (C110S), that selectively abrogates PPI-Eya to show that PPI-Eya is necessary for the transcriptional activity of So in cultured cells and to promote eye formation in Drosophila. Using heterologous leucine zipper domains, we specifically reconstituted the So{Delta}Eya-Eya PPI and show that this complex is transcriptionally active in cells and can rescue eye development. PPI-Rescue was also used to restore transcriptional activity to So{Delta}PPI (V111E), an allele that mimics the human SIX1(V17E) allele associated with Branchio-Oto-Renal syndrome. PPI-Rescue thus represents an innovative approach to understanding the complex molecular logic of transcription complexes in both development and disease.

last_author.name: Neal, S. J.
last_author.affiliation: SUNY Upstate Medical University

preprints.title: PatHoST: weakly supervised reconstruction of pathogen spatial distributions from host transcriptomes
preprints.abstract: Dual host-pathogen spatial transcriptomics enables spatially resolved investigation of infection, yet the completeness of pathogen detection remains poorly characterized. Here, we generated pathogen-only spatial transcriptomic sections from a chronic Mycobacterium abscessus lung infection model to experimentally benchmark pathogen detection, revealing substantially increased pathogen transcript recovery compared with conventional dual profiling. Building on these data, we developed PatHoST, a weakly supervised computational framework that uses pathogen-derived information to generate silver-standard labels and learns host transcriptional programs predictive of pathogen presence. PatHoST reconstructed pathogen spatial distributions across independent tissue sections and enabled the identification of localized host regulatory programs beyond conventional cluster-based analyses. Application to human SARS-CoV-2 lung spatial transcriptomics supported generalization across host species and pathogen classes. Together, PatHoST combines purpose-built experimental benchmarking with weakly supervised inference to recover latent pathogen information and extend the analytical capabilities of dual host-pathogen spatial transcriptomics.

preprints.title: Polycomb Marked Promoter Methylation Gains in Aging and Cancer are Independent of Replication
preprints.abstract: DNA methylation alterations are hallmark features of aging and cancer, occurring early during tumor initiation. Yet how these changes evolve during early tumorigenesis, and whether oncogenic signaling actively drives them, remains poorly understood due to limitations in resolving this at the longitudinal and clonal level. Here we developed a genome-wide DNA methylation profiling method for low DNA amounts and applied it to single stem cell-derived clones from a BRAFV600E -inducible mouse colon organoid model, tracking nucleotide-level methylation heterogeneity over time. BRAFV600E induction produced stepwise methylation divergence consistent with progressive clonal takeover, in contrast to gradual epigenetic drift in uninduced controls. Strikingly, while the specific CpG sites altered differed between BRAFV600E and control lineages, they converged on the same genomic elements. Particularly, Polycomb-marked promoter CpG-island methylation gains were not induced or accelerated by BRAFV600E, challenging models in which oncogenic signaling or cell proliferation actively instructs de novo methylation of Polycomb-targeted promoters. Instead, these gains tracked with "biological aging" independent of replication, which was validated across independent aging, cancer, and cell-line datasets. BRAFV600E -induced clones additionally showed progressive loss of intestinal lineage-specification transcription factor programs, consistent with selection for cells adapted to oncogenic stress. Together, these findings show that epigenetic trajectories during early tumor development, are rooted in baseline, age-dependent drivers of epigenetic alterations, and that oncogenic signaling acts primarily by selecting and expanding clones bearing pre-existing, age-associated epigenetic drift rather than instructing new methylation. Our findings have implications for how promoter methylation is interpreted as a cancer biomarker and for identifying upstream aging-associated processes as targets for early intervention.

preprints.title: Resolving how genetic perturbations act through gene regulatory paths
preprints.abstract: Perturb-seq measures transcriptional responses to thousands of genetic perturbations, but each gene's response mixes the contributions of many regulatory paths, so how a perturbation acts cannot be resolved from expression alone, however large the model. Here we present REGA-perturb, which supplies this missing information rather than adding model complexity: reference epigenomes define a scaffold of possible transcription factor (TF)-regulatory element-gene paths, and perturbation responses, pooled through shared latent programs, determine how each path is used, requiring only RNA measurements. Across three CRISPR interference screens totaling 2.4 million cells, REGA-perturb inferred TF-target relationships that agreed with ChIP-seq binding with a gain over random more than four times that of the best existing method, separated candidate direct from indirect targets, and predicted targets of TFs withheld from training. It also inferred perturbation-induced changes in TF activity not reflected in TF transcript levels, and resolved perturbation-specific regulatory rewiring in which opposing regulatory changes cancel at the expression level.

last_author.name: Duren, Z.
last_author.affiliation: Indiana University School of Medicine

preprints.title: Simulating the dynamics of gene regulatory systems at cellular scale
preprints.abstract: The temporal nature of eukaryotic gene expression is the result of a complex, non-linear, dynamical system of regulatory processes. So far, models of such systems trade realism for tractability by using strict simplifying assumptions. These simplified models are often unfaithful to our biological understanding; however, without such simplifications, analytical solutions become more challenging and these dynamical systems must then be studied through simulation. Here, we explore the question of how this complex web of gene regulatory connections can be faithfully simulated for all tens of thousands of genes that usually define a eukaryotic organism. We present a proof-of-principle model and simulator, GeneRegulatorySystems.jl which is based on a biophysical chemical master equation that overcomes three key restrictions. First, it allows an exact stochastic simulation of fully non-linear gene expression dynamics, including feedback control, to parsimoniously capture cause and effect relationships of gene regulation. Further, it includes a general framework for implementing diverse mechanisms of gene control such as protein mediated degradation, RNAi, and protein complex formation. Finally, it scales realistically to tens of thousands of genes. We achieve this by introducing a domain-specific programming language to aid the design of experimental protocols from small-scale, well-studied, scenarios of gene regulation inspired by dynamical systems biology up to large-scale, single cell omics experiments with interventions. In this way, our framework provides a grammar of in silico experimental design that can capture single-cell gene expression dynamics for entire genomes.

preprints.title: Spatiotemporal mapping of endothelial proliferative response in acute chemical liver injury
preprints.abstract: Endothelial cells are major contributors to liver injury response, regeneration, and chronic liver disease. Previous studies identified a proliferative endothelial response to acute liver injury; however, a comprehensive characterization of this adaptive response is missing. We have developed a novel pipeline for spatiotemporal analysis of proliferative response in the liver. We demonstrate that endothelial cells enter the cell cycle upon acute centrilobular injury with a delay compared to hepatocytes and in a spatially distinct pattern from hepatocytes. We show that endothelial cycling predominantly occurs in the pericentral zone, while hepatocyte cycling occurs uniformly throughout the lobule. Endothelial cycling in injured livers leads to heightened clonal expansion, and to serial division rarely observed in homeostatic livers. Consequently, injured lobules exhibit endothelial overabundance during regeneration. Our study provides an in-depth characterization of endothelial proliferative response to liver injury and establishes a novel pipeline for spatiotemporal mapping of hepatic cell states.

preprints.title: Spectral Adaptive Repositioning for Flow-Based Single-Cell Perturbation Modeling
preprints.abstract: Predicting transcriptome-wide cellular responses to genetic and biomolecular perturbations is central to functional genomics and therapeutic target discovery. Existing methods assign gene positional encodings derived from arbitrary orderings or static co-expression masks built from unperturbed cells, and cannot capture the functional rewiring induced by perturbations. We present SPEAR, a generative framework built on two complementary positional mechanisms. Spectral positional encoding grounds each gene's position in the geometry of the co-expression network via continuous coordinates derived from the graph Laplacian. Adaptive repositioning then derives each gene's position from its perturbation-conditioned hidden state at every layer, allowing the attention genes exert on one another to reorganize without explicit supervision. Evaluated on genetic, pharmacological, and cytokine perturbation benchmarks, SPEAR demonstrates excellent recovery of differential gene-expression, distributional structure, and perturbation-specific identifiability. SPEAR also captures latent positional relationships that closely map to known transcription factor-target interactions. https://github.com/shouryaverma/SPEAR}{https://github.com/shouryaverma/SPEAR

preprints.title: Structure-Function Analysis of an Infantile Rhabdomyosarcoma Fusion-Oncogene Reveals Domain Requirements for Tumorigenesis
preprints.abstract: Rhabdomyosarcoma is a pediatric soft-tissue sarcoma that reflects impaired skeletal muscle differentiation. Spindle cell/sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma is a histological subtype found in children and adults. In children under two, spindle cell rhabdomyosarcoma is genetically driven by fusion-oncogenes of transcription factors or co-activators important for skeletal muscle lineage commitment and development. The most common fusion-oncogene in this group is VGLL2::NCOA2, a fusion between vestigial-like family member 2 (VGLL2) and nuclear receptor coactivator 2 (NCOA2). Children with fusion-driven rhabdomyosarcoma are treated with general chemotherapy, surgery, and radiation, which are not specific to the molecular underpinnings, and increase risk of secondary malignancies and premature death. Previously, we showed that VGLL2::NCOA2 is transforming in mouse myoblasts and transgenic zebrafish tumor models. Here, we build on this work by detailing the structure-function relationship of the retained VGLL2::NCOA2 protein domains to define domain requirements and their molecular interactions for tumorigenesis. We created deletion mutants of the VGLL2 vestigial/Tondu (TDU) domain and the NCOA2 activating domains 1 and 2 (AD1 and AD2), and a double mutant lacking the TDU+AD1 domains and assessed their function in a mouse myoblast model. We find that the TDU and AD1 domains support nuclear fusion-oncogene localization, transformation in vitro, and tumorigenesis in a mouse allograft model. Furthermore, transcriptomic analysis demonstrates that the TDU or AD1 mutant VGLL2::NCOA2 drives an upregulation of myogenesis gene sets and supports terminal differentiation. Overall, our results indicate that VGLL2::NCOA2 requires the TDU and AD1 domains for optimal transformation, and that targeting these domains, or their interacting protein partners, represents a therapeutic opportunity.

last_author.name: Kendall, G. C.

preprints.title: Temporal genomic imprinting regulates grain filling in barley
preprints.abstract: In cereals, the persistent endosperm accumulates starch and storage proteins, making their grains a major source of food and feed. Early grain development is epigenetically controlled through the parent-of-origin-specific expression of imprinted genes in the endosperm that regulate endosperm proliferation, nutrient accumulation and embryo nourishment. Imprinted genes have been identified in several major cereals, and a few have been functionally characterized. However, it is unclear how imprinted genes regulate the accumulation of storage compounds in cereal grains. Through spatiotemporal transcriptome analysis of 255 imprinted genes in barley (Hordeum vulgare), we identify endosperm transfer cells in grains as a hotspot of expression of imprinted genes. Furthermore, we show that transcription factor LYS3 dynamically regulates grain filling in barley through early expression of the maternal allele, followed by partial activation of the paternal allele.
