preprints.title: Analysis of sperm processing and cryopreservation procedures in the common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus) to reduce fragmentation and maximize total and progressive motility
preprints.abstract: The marmoset has emerged as an ideal species for studying complex neurodevelopmental diseases, and IVF is required for gene-editing success. Reliable sperm processing is paramount to several IVF techniques, including traditional insemination. If not used immediately, thermal stress from cryopreservation diminishes sperm quality, requiring improved processing methods. Swim-up and gradient methods may limit adequate sperm quality, and the lack of a standardized freezing protocol often results in impaired post-thaw motility. Thus, reliable standards for sperm processing and cryopreservation in the marmoset are needed to support vital IVF processes. Collected semen underwent one of four pre-processing incubation steps before processing by swim-up, sucrose gradient, or a microfluidics assay. Sperm parameters were assessed using a Hamilton Thorne Computer Assisted Sperm Analysis (CASA) system. To evaluate cryopreservation, microfluidics-processed sperm were subjected to five protocols using different cryoprotectants and cooling methods. After thawing, sperm samples were analyzed with the CASA system and a DNA fragmentation assay. Incubation for 30 minutes at 38C in TYH media decreased sperm aggregation, and subsequent microfluidics resulted in a higher percentage of motile and progressively motile sperm than swim-up or gradient methods. Our optimized cryopreservation protocol consistently achieved at least 20% progressive motility, a key benchmark for usable marmoset sperm, while previously published or commercial methods were less consistent. The cryopreservation protocol outperformed other published methods, having the least significant change in post-thaw motility without causing DNA damage. These findings establish standardized methods for reliably procuring and storing sperm samples for IVF or husbandry in the common marmoset.

preprints.title: Autonomous generalizability auditing of scientific foundation models
preprints.abstract: Determining where scientific foundation models generalize beyond their development data is essential for reliable use, but aggregate benchmarks obscure performance limits and rigorous audits are difficult to conduct routinely. Here, we introduce AutoSPECTRA, a coding-agent protocol for systematic generalizability auditing. To inform its design, we reviewed 38 studies across five biological domains and evaluated coding agents, which generated hypotheses and empirical analyses but applied inconsistent standards for judging evidence. We then structured AutoSPECTRA around measurable generalization axes, prespecified analyses, controlled comparisons and independent confirmation. Across four biological foundation models, audits linked performance to protein sequence composition and relatedness to pretraining data (ESMFold2), representation of perturbations in training (STATE), effective spatial resolution (CONCH), and residue-level genomic, evolutionary and structural context (AlphaMissense). Agents also evaluated alternative explanations and rejected unsupported hypotheses. AutoSPECTRA provides a systematic approach to discovering and testing the limits of scientific foundation models.

preprints.title: BSG.S regulates ionocyte radial intercalation and function in the developing Xenopus mucociliary epithelium.
preprints.abstract: Mucociliary epithelia (MCE) line multiple vertebrate organs, including the mammalian airways, and rely on coordinated interactions among specialized cell types to clear pathogens and maintain epithelial homeostasis. Proper MCE function requires the appropriate specification and spatial organization of ionocytes, multiciliated cells, secretory cells, and basal cells. Ionocytes regulate ion transport and pH homeostasis, yet the mechanisms governing their integration and function within the developing epithelium remain incompletely understood. Basigin (BSG), also known as CD147 or EMMPRIN, is a conserved transmembrane glycoprotein implicated in cell migration, adhesion, and signaling. However, its role in mucociliary epithelial development remains unclear. Here, we show that the short isoform of BSG (BSG.S) is expressed in ionocytes of the Xenopus laevis MCE. Our findings demonstrate that BSG.S depletion impairs ionocyte radial intercalation, alters intracellular pH, and disrupts epithelial organization. Furthermore, BSG.S loss alters epithelial cell-type composition, decreasing the number of basal cells and increasing the number of multiciliated cells. These findings suggest BSG.S as a regulator of ionocyte integration, epithelial organization, and cell-type composition during mucociliary epithelial development.

last_author.name: Yoon, J.
last_author.affiliation: National Cancer Institute (NCI)

preprints.title: Bioactivity foundation model for hit identification and hit-to-lead optimization from sequence data
preprints.abstract: Learning from large-scale bioactivity archives is complicated by heterogeneous assay readouts and differences in data reliability. Here we show that a model that predicts probability distributions over binding affinities from sequence data opens model training to vast and diverse troves of heterogeneous bioactivity data. We develop PSICHIC+, a bioactivity foundation model trained on approximately 82 million protein-ligand records using a distributional objective that preserves quantitative resolution while incorporating variation in data reliability. Given a protein sequence and ligand SMILES, PSICHIC+ predicts binding affinity in milliseconds. In zero-shot virtual-screening benchmarks without target-specific training data, it improves enrichment over regression- and classification-based approaches and performs competitively with leading structure-based methods. In lab-in-the-loop campaigns, distribution-guided acquisition improves recovery of high-activity compounds under fixed screening budgets. Combining PSICHIC+ with Boltz-2 improves hit-to-lead affinity prediction over Boltz-2 alone, with mean correlation approaching that of FEP+ on the evaluated benchmarks, without requiring high-resolution protein structures. These results support distributional learning as a scalable approach to using heterogeneous bioactivity data for hit identification and hit-to-lead optimization.

preprints.title: CARTnet: Template-guided B-cell Epitope Prediction with Contact-aware Attention
preprints.abstract: B-cell epitope prediction remains challenging due to the limited availability of experimentally characterized data and the incomplete understanding of antibody-antigen recognition. Here, we present CARTnet, a novel contact-aware deep learning framework that integrates multimodal features and template-derived epitope information. CARTnet demonstrated superior performance when compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods across most evaluation metrics on both the internal and external test datasets. In particular, CARTnet achieved an AUPRC of 0.243 on the internal test set, compared with 0.220 for DiscoTope-3, 0.140 for BepiPred-2, and 0.198 for BepiPred-3. This improvement was also observed on the external test set, where CARTnet achieved an AUPRC of 0.267, compared with 0.192, 0.111, and 0.215 for DiscoTope-3, BepiPred-2, and BepiPred-3, respectively, supporting its generalizability. CARTnet also supports template-guided prediction, in which limited prior epitope information can improve the identification of additional epitope residues; a single template residue increased the AUPRC of the template-based variant from 0.225 to 0.403 on the internal test set. Furthermore, we demonstrated that epitope information from closely related viruses can be transferred across the genus Alphavirus to improve epitope prediction accuracy. These results establish CARTnet as an accurate framework for both de novo and template-guided B-cell epitope prediction.

preprints.title: Cellular composition and the interpretation of candidate RNA readouts of trogocytosis in colorectal cancer
preprints.abstract: Background: RNA measurements of genes associated with trogocytosis may reflect cellular composition rather than contact-dependent membrane acquisition. We evaluated an eight-gene candidate module in colorectal cancer (CRC) using expression- and lineage-matched random modules, independent compartment analysis and patient-level inference. A separate rare-transcript definition and cancer-model fitness screens provided complementary analyses. Results: In 62 GSE178341 patients, the module correlated with T-cell fraction ({rho}=0.767), but this association was typical of 10,000 matched modules (null median 0.766; one-sided empirical P=0.493; equal-tail two-sided P=0.985). A post hoc closest-10% matching sensitivity gave P=0.571. In 23 independent GSE132465 patients, the tumour-wide correlation was 0.735 (permutation P=0.00060) and the epithelial correlation was 0.376 (P=0.0892). The difference in absolute correlations was 0.359, with a 95% confidence interval of -0.041 to 0.759, leaving attenuation uncertain. Among 43,817 leukocytes, 16 CEACAM5-positive candidates arose from four patients; 15 had expression [≤]2 transcripts per million. Candidate counts were threshold-sensitive. No survival association was detected for the module in two cohorts. SCD fitness dependency reproduced across CRC organoids and cell lines, whereas adjusted SCD-VPS72 and exploratory ATF3-SMYD2 co-dependencies did not. Exploratory CH25H, ATF3 and FADS2 analyses yielded no Hallmark enrichment meeting the multiple-testing threshold. Conclusions: Matched-module calibration placed the strong association with T-cell abundance within the range expected for comparable immune-lineage genes. Independent compartment analysis was consistent with a contribution from cellular composition, although attenuation remained uncertain. These results identify the comparison conditions needed to interpret the tested RNA readouts. Linking them to membrane transfer requires event-resolved protein measurements.
preprints.corresponding_institution: The Affiliated Hospital of Guizhou Medical University

preprints.title: Classifying tumors from broad category to hierarchical molecular subtype: an interpretable hierarchical framework for precision oncology
preprints.abstract: Precise tumor subtype classification is important for guiding personalized treatment, characterizing tumor heterogeneity, and investigating molecular mechanisms. However, most existing multi-label classification models use flat architectures and do not fully exploit the inherent hierarchical relationships and biological constraints among tumor types, which limits their performance and interpretability in complex, fine-grained pan-cancer classification. Here, we present the cancer Hallmark-based Hierarchical Recursive Model (HHRM) for pan-cancer hierarchical multi-label classification. HHRM integrates hierarchical label structures with recursive neural networks, enabling simultaneous modeling of multi-level dependencies from broad cancer categories to specific subtypes. We trained the model on a comprehensive pan-cancer cohort of 11,476 samples spanning 26 primary cancer types and 405 subtypes across up to eight hierarchical levels. HHRM achieved an accuracy of 0.7924 for predicting hierarchical tumor subtypes and was further evaluated on a validation dataset of 887 samples. Compared with other hierarchical modeling frameworks, HHRM achieved higher accuracy in all three output modes. Ablation experiments showed that replacing the hallmark-based graph convolutional network reduced model performance. On an independent dataset of 1,608 breast cancer samples, HHRM also achieved an accuracy greater than 0.86. Finally, we combined SHAP with a network-based method to rank and analyze predictive genes at different levels of the tumor hierarchy, which identified both known and potentially novel biomarkers for cancer diagnosis. In conclusion, to our knowledge, HHRM is the first hierarchical model for multi-level tumor subtype classification. Its competitive performance, combined with post hoc biological interpretation, suggests potential value for precision cancer diagnosis.

last_author.name: Lai, X.
last_author.affiliation: Tampere University

preprints.title: Coding region changes in the Hippo pathway component YAP1 contribute to body size differences among mammalian species
preprints.abstract: Animal species differ dramatically in their overall size, yet the mechanisms underlying these differences are poorly understood. The Hippo pathway, first discovered in Drosophila, and widely conserved in mammals, regulates the nuclear levels of YAP1, a transcriptional co-activator that enhances the expression of growth-promoting genes. While experimental manipulations of this pathway elicit dramatic effects on tissue growth and organ size, it is not known whether, and to what extent, evolutionary divergence of this pathway has contributed to size differences across animals. Here we show that although YAP1 protein sequence is highly conserved between diverse mammals such as humans, elephants and blue whales, it diverges considerably among rodent species. While the human YAP1 protein is very similar to that of the largest rodent, the capybara Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris, those of smaller rodents such as the mouse Mus musculus and the vole Microtus oregoni show considerable divergence. An increased ratio of non-synonymous versus synonymous substitutions (dN/dS) in clades of small rodents compared to the background is indicative of relaxed constraint in these lineages, suggesting relative positive selection. When expressed in the developing Drosophila wing, capybara YAP1 was more potent at promoting growth than that of the mouse or vole. Following transfection into mammalian cells, capybara YAP1 is more effective at promoting expression of a reporter gene than either mouse or vole YAP1. Thus, by combining computational and experimental approaches, we show that evolutionarily divergent coding-region changes in YAP1 have likely contributed to the evolution of smaller body size in clades of rodents.

last_author.name: Hariharan, I. K.
last_author.affiliation: University of California, Berkeley

preprints.title: Comparative Transcriptomic Analysis of Gene Expression Patterns in Neutrophils from Rheumatoid Arthritis and COVID-19
preprints.abstract: Background: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disorder characterised by chronic inflammation and immune dysregulation, and neutrophils play a key role in its progression. COVID-19 also involves neutrophil hyperactivation that contributes to severe immune responses. Emerging evidence links COVID-19 to increased incidence or exacerbation of RA, potentially through overlapping immune mechanisms. Objective: To compare neutrophil transcriptomic profiles in RA and COVID-19 and identify shared immune pathways and disease-specific features. Methods: Publicly available neutrophil RNA-seq count data from the Gene Expression Omnibus were analysed: RA versus healthy controls (GSE116899) and COVID-19 versus healthy controls (GSE212041). A second COVID-19 comparison (severe versus convalescent) was assembled from GSE272381 and GSE227116. Differential expression was analysed with DESeq2, pathway enrichment with fgsea (Hallmark gene sets) and topGO (Gene Ontology biological process and molecular function). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were compared between diseases by direction of change. Results: In RA neutrophils, 11,355 DEGs were identified, of which 90 had an absolute log2 fold change of at least 2 with p<0.05 (70 upregulated, 20 downregulated). Twenty-four Hallmark gene sets were positively enriched at adjusted p<0.05, led by interferon alpha and interferon gamma responses, and Gene Ontology analysis highlighted type I interferon, antiviral and double-stranded RNA terms. In COVID-19 neutrophils, 420 DEGs were identified (37 upregulated, 383 downregulated), and no Hallmark gene set reached adjusted p<0.05. Of the 90 RA DEGs, 46 changed in the same direction in COVID-19 without reaching significance, and 27 changed significantly in the opposite direction, including CAMK1G, SIGLEC1, OAS1 and OAS3. In the second COVID-19 comparison, several of these genes, including OAS1, OAS3 and SIGLEC1, changed in the same direction as in RA. Conclusions: RA neutrophils show a transcriptional programme enriched for interferon and antiviral-response pathways. Part of the RA signature is shared with COVID-19 neutrophils, while a subset of genes diverges, and this divergence depended on the COVID-19 comparison used. These findings are hypothesis-generating and provide candidate genes for experimental validation.

preprints.title: Context, not contradiction: a pan-cancer framework for conforming and nonconforming co-expression programmes
preprints.abstract: Reports of a gene's role in cancer frequently conflict: the same transcript is described as an adverse prognostic marker in one tumour type and a favourable one in another, and such discordance is usually attributed to cohort differences or to irreproducibility. An alternative explanation is that the transcriptional company a gene keeps genuinely differs between lineages. That claim is testable, but testing it requires separating real lineage-dependence from three artefacts that pervade pan-cancer co-expression analysis: public summaries report only coefficients above a fixed threshold, a gene in a recurrently gained region acquires correlates through dosage alone, and conservation across cancer types is assumed rather than measured. We present a framework that addresses all three for any index gene. Correlations are recomputed threshold-free from each cohort's expression matrix; transcripts are partitioned into cis and trans sets relative to the index gene after retired symbols are resolved; a recurrence rule freezes the gene set before any downstream analysis; cohorts are scored against expression-decile-matched permutation nulls; and copy number is residualised out using the cis set as a built-in positive control, so the adjustment is shown to work before the trans result is read. Applied to PTK2, encoding focal adhesion kinase, across 17 TCGA cohorts, expression was associated with poor outcome in several cancers and better outcome in others, independently of tumour purity. The framework shows this is not noise: cohorts separate into conforming and nonconforming groups enriched for different biology. The 44-transcript trans programme is unchanged by copy-number adjustment while the cis control collapses by 38%, and co-expression is recoverable within individual tumours in 133 of 243 single-cell cases.

last_author.name: Stupack, D. G.
last_author.affiliation: UCSD-Moores Cancer Center

preprints.title: Continuous Topological Accessibility (RFA) as a 3D-Aware GRN Filter: Anticorrelation with eQTL and No Prediction of ΔRNA
preprints.abstract: We formalize Relative Forest Accessibility (RFA), a topological accessibility index computed as the solution of (I - {gamma}P )x = v0, where P is a Markov transition matrix built from Hi-C contacts and v0 is a vector of TF peaks (or ATAC peaks). RFA yields a continuous accessibility profile across all genomic bins. We test RFA on three targets. First, on promoter TF counts (GM12878 chr1, 10 kb, 811 genes), RFA loses to 1D distance (AUC 0.836 vs 0.976); this is an artifact because the target and the 1D distance look at the same window. Second, on eQTL (GTEx v10 LCL, chr1+17+19, 10 kb, 1625 genes), RFA anticorrelates with eQTL: {rho}(RFA, - log10 pmin) = -0.09, AUC(RFA) = 0.386 (below chance), AUC(-RFA) = 0.614. High RFA corresponds to fewer eQTL, and dose-response analysis confirms that AUC(RFA) decreases with eQTL strength (mean trend -0.056, 19/20 TFs). A distance-preserving shuffle of the Hi-C matrix reproduces this anticorrelation ({triangleup}AUC vs real: [-0.074, +0.076] across 5 TFs, all CIs include 0), whereas a degree-preserving rewiring destroys it ({triangleup}AUC [isin] [-0.261, -0.003], CIs exclude 0 for 5/5 TFs); the anticorrelation therefore reflects distance-decay of Hi-C contacts (local 3D accessibility), not higher-order topology. The anticorrelation replicates on chr17 ({triangleup}{rho} = -0.13 for rewired, 0/5 for shuffled) and on chr19 with an inverted control pattern, consistent with local within-diagonal heterogeneity as the carrier on short gene-dense chromosomes. Third, on {triangleup}RNA (MCF10A vs MCF7, 40 kb, ATAC peaks), RFA does not predict {triangleup}RNA ({rho} = +0.005, permutation p = 0.87, bootstrap 95% CI [-0.040, +0.053], n = 1730); the CI includes zero and does not exclude the practical boundary |{rho}| = 0.05. Within-line sanity checks are also null. We conclude that RFA anticorrelates with eQTL via local distance-decay and does not predict {triangleup}RNA. The anticorrelation is carried by distance-decay, not by loops or TADs, and may reflect expression buffering: genes with strong eQTL are less dependent on local 3D accessibility. RFA is not a universal predictor but a filter with an inverted sign on eQTL and no signal on {triangleup}RNA.

preprints.title: Cross-cancer knowledge transfer for lymph node metastasis prediction: Applicability of an axillary lymph node-based deep learning model
preprints.abstract: Evaluation of lymph node (LN) metastasis is critical for cancer staging and treatment planning. Since radiologic hallmarks of metastatic LNs are shared across primary cancers, a computed tomography (CT)-based deep learning (DL) classifier developed from one anatomy may transfer to others. This study built a DenseNet-121 ensemble model using clinical-implication-applied preprocessing and evaluated its cross-anatomical generalizability to LNs from diverse primary cancers. A DenseNet-121 ensemble model combining fixed-size cropping (FSC) and adjustable square cropping (ASC) was trained from ImageNet initialization on an axillary lymph node (ALN) dataset (n = 1,128 from 523 breast cancer patients). The model utilized clinical-implication-applied perinodal cropping with bicubic filtering and standardized resizing. To test cross-anatomical generalizability, an external dataset of 256 CT images across four anatomical regions was evaluated: cervical, mediastinal, upper-abdominal, and lower-abdominal LNs. Perinodal free margins were systematically varied from 10% to 40% to optimize the balance between context preservation and surround interference. Bicubic filtering and standardized resizing yielded the highest internal performance on the original ALN dataset (FSC-ASC ensemble area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.958, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.920-0.987 at 40% margin). The model demonstrated site-dependent, above-chance generalizability across all external regions. Cervical LNs achieved the highest performance at a 40% margin (AUROC 0.939, 95% CI 0.875-0.989). Mediastinal LNs peaked at a 10% margin (AUROC 0.796, 95% CI 0.672-0.903), with wider margins degrading performance due to adjacent structural interference. Upper-abdominal and lower-abdominal LNs reached optimal performance at a 30% margin (AUROC 0.814 for upper; AUROC 0.917 for lower). A single ALN-trained DL model can accurately predict LN metastasis across cervical, mediastinal, and abdominal stations through site-specific perinodal margin tuning. These findings support the feasibility of cross-cancer knowledge transfer and the clinical utility of generalizable backbones for pan-cancer nodal assessment.

last_author.name: Kim, B. J.

preprints.title: DEEPNET-LLM: Highly accurate structure prediction of unknown metabolites from mass spectra via their molecular neighborhoods
preprints.abstract: Most molecular features detected by untargeted mass spectrometry-based metabolomics remain unannotated. This so-called 'dark matter' currently comprises more than 90% and likely holds uncharacterized bioactive chemistry. Structure prediction from fragmentation spectra remains an outstanding challenge, because a spectrum does not uniquely determine a structure and the space of candidate structures is mostly unbounded; correspondingly, existing methods rarely return the correct de novo structure as their top prediction. Here we describe De novo Ego network-Enabled Propagation and Neighborhood Extrapolation of Topology using Large Language Models (DEEPNET-LLM) reasoning approach, which uses Molecular Community Networking (MCN) to restrict the search of a query spectrum to its local neighborhood within the global metabolome, and applies AI reasoning to propagate structural information from neighbors to the query. For a collection of 900 authentic standards (2,249 spectra) that have never been publicly released to exclude possibility of data leakage, DEEPNET-LLM returned the correct structure as its top prediction for 84.7% of spectra. Accuracy was independent of precursor mass across a range over which the number of candidate structures grows by 30 orders of magnitude, and was comparable across ion polarity, adducts and in-source fragmentation. On a random subset of the public MassSpecGym benchmark, DEEPNET-LLM reached 85.9% top-1 accuracy excluding stereochemistry. We showcase the use of DEEPNET-LLM with an example of a discovery of tryptamine amidate of a bile acid in mouse gut, confirmed against a synthetic standard. The DEEPNET-LLM approach is orthogonal to existing in silico methods and can be combined with them.

last_author.name: Aksenov, A. A.

preprints.title: DUET: sequence-only prediction of RNA-small molecule binding sites
preprints.abstract: Sequence-only predictors can score RNA-small-molecule binding sites without the need to obtain experimental RNA structures, but reported performance can be confounded by test-homologous training records and by inconsistent treatment of within-training redundancy. We introduce DUET, a sequence-only ensemble, and evaluate it with a test-clean protocol that controls these effects separately. Test-homologous records are removed, whereas sequence-identical training records are grouped into homology components and size-balanced to prevent family dominance. Across 10 paired seeds, DUET reached 0.240 {+/-} 0.013 MCC, compared with 0.192 {+/-} 0.031 for CoBRA-M3 trained on the same data (Delta = +0.047). Increasing the training pool from 80 to 290 records raised DUET by +0.135 MCC. DUET also reached 0.246 MCC on two independent SMARTPocket sets, supporting transport beyond the benchmark source. DUET is implemented in Python and PyTorch. Source code, manifests, processed graphs, trained checkpoints and scripts that regenerate the results are available at https://github.com/xiong-0212/DUET and archived at Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.23635381).

preprints.title: De novo genome assembly of the floating-hook moss Warnstorfia fluitans
preprints.abstract: The floating-hook moss Warnstorfia fluitans is a natural species dominant in subarctic and Arctic aquatic ecosystems. It is adapted to cold, acidic, and nutrient-deficient environments and possesses great potential for bioremediation by removing contaminants from polluted water in cold climate conditions. Here, we present the first de novo genome assembly of W. fluitans generated from pooled male and female gametophytes. The assembly is 725.04 Mb, has a N50 of 193.5 kb, a BUSCO completeness of 97.6% against the Viridiplantae lineage and 82% against the Embryophyta lineage. The whole assembly has Merqury quality value of 37 and Merqury completeness of 92%. A total of 30421 protein coding genes were predicted, with 78.62% completeness by compleasm and 87% OMArk completeness against the Embryophyta lineage. Repetitive sequences comprise 56.16% of the genome. We also present here the two complete circular chloroplast genomes and a linear mitochondrial genome of W. fluitans. This genomic resource will facilitate studies of ecological adaptation and a wide range of biological and evolutionary studies in bryophytes.

preprints.title: Delta/Notch signaling level is decoded through transcriptional burst duration during muscle progenitor specification
preprints.abstract: The ability of progenitor cells to interpret different levels of signaling pathway activity is fundamental to the generation of cellular diversity during development. Muscle progenitors, for example, are exposed to different levels of signals from their microenvironment. However, how they decode these quantitative differences to regulate their cellular behaviors during myogenesis remains poorly understood. Here, we addressed this question during the specification of two populations of Drosophila adult muscle progenitors (AMPs). We found that, despite being spatially adjacent, indirect flight muscle (IFM) and direct flight muscle (DFM) progenitors receive distinct levels of Notch signaling. We further show that the spatial distribution of epithelial Delta contributes to differential Notch activation. Higher Delta levels adjacent to IFM progenitors promote stronger Notch signaling. To investigate how these quantitative differences are translated into transcriptional responses, we developed a Notch-responsive MS2 reporter to monitor transcription in living AMPs. Our measurements reveal that Notch-dependent transcription occurs in stochastic bursts, with IFM progenitors displaying longer but less frequent bursts than DFM progenitors. Strikingly, equalizing epithelial Delta levels abolished differences between the two populations in both Notch-dependent transcriptional activity and the protein levels of Notch target genes. Together, our findings suggest that quantitative differences in signaling may be translated into distinct transcriptional outputs through modulation of transcriptional bursting. This may represent a mechanism by which a single signaling pathway can be deployed to regulate diverse cellular responses during development.

preprints.title: Dietary fibre responses emerge through host-dietary regime interplay: Apple pectin modulates immune reactivity in adult zebrafish
preprints.abstract: Dietary fibres are rarely consumed independently. Instead, they form part of an overall diet that includes dietary fibres from different sources, in varying amounts and consumed under different feeding patterns. Here, we tested how dietary regimes containing apple pectin, oat {beta}-glucan, or cellulose shaped the host. We analysed gut microbiome composition by 16S rRNA sequencing, measured brain and intestinal SCFA profiles by targeted metabolomics, and assessed immunomodulation by measuring gene expression systemically in the blood and locally in the spleen, as well as intestinal enzyme activity. The dietary intervention was conducted for 12 weeks on adult female and male zebrafish (Danio rerio). Our results show that the gut microbial composition can be relatively stable across different dietary fibre exposure patterns yet still vary significantly between the sexes. Additionally, the effect of sex on the gut microbiome may become more evident when dietary fibres are administered at high dosages, but intermittently. Dietary fibre regimes can alter intestinal short-chain fatty acid profiles more readily than brain profiles, which show a stronger sexually dimorphic response. Interestingly, apple pectin modulated the zebrafish immune response through interactions dependent on the overall regime, tissue, sex, and host immune status. Notably, tissue il1b gene expression differed depending on how apple pectin was administered and the host's physiological state. Collectively, our study emphasises the highly context-specific effects of dietary fibres, shaped by the dynamic interplay between the overall dietary regime and intertwined host factors.

last_author.name: Immler, S.

preprints.title: Digital twins forecast individual immune trajectories
preprints.abstract: The human immune system differs markedly between individuals and changes in response to infection, vaccination and treatment. AI virtual cells are being built to simulate cellular responses to perturbation. Yet these models, like most immune-response predictors, describe each person by a single pre-challenge measurement and forecast change from patterns pooled across people. Digital twins, updated with every new observation of an individual, could forecast how that person's immune state changes. Here we present ImmuneTwins, which builds these twins from single-cell profiles by personalizing a shared virtual-cell model with each individual's observations. In two external populations, ImmuneTwins reduced immune-age error by 32% and 42% relative to the best existing method. During repeated influenza vaccination, its twins predicted the direction of immune-cell change 35% more accurately than the best published method, and their error fell by 27% as observations accumulated. The twins revealed that immune cells and plasma proteins recover about half their deviation from a persistent personal reference within 90 days, whereas response size varies between challenges. They further localized B-cell remodelling in exceptional longevity and anticipated patient-specific immune trajectories during myeloma treatment. These results establish virtual-cell digital twins for forecasting individual immune change and identifying each person's characteristic immune features.

last_author.name: Chen, C. Y.-C.

preprints.title: Does a map-level insulation constraint improve sequence-based prediction of 3D genome folding? A Stage 1 Registered Report with a reverse-complement-equivariant state-space model (HiFold-Mamba)
preprints.abstract: Background. Sequence-to-contact-map models are trained with pixel-wise losses, although the features of interest (insulation, domain boundaries, loops) are summaries of the map. Insulationbased losses help Hi-C resolution enhancement. No pre-specified test has asked whether they improve sequence-based prediction, judged against annotations independent of the training data. Proposed study. HiFold-Mamba predicts 448 x 448 maps at 2,048 bp from 1,048,576 bp of DNA on the DNALongBench contact-map task. Every component is reverse-complement-equivariant: convolutional tower, bidirectional Mamba blocks, multi-scale mixer and symmetric pairwise head. We pre-register three hypotheses: >> H1: it exceeds each of three trained baselines (reproduced Akita, a parameter-matched Transformer and a parameter-matched CNN) by [≥]0.01 stratum-adjusted correlation (SCC). >> H2: an insulation and boundary loss, computed from the predicted map with the operator used on the observed map, improves boundary AUROC and loop AP against independent 4DN boundary calls and ENCODE CTCF ChIA-PET loops, at equal training steps and without loss of SCC. >> H3: pretraining plus few-shot adaptation beats training from scratch on four held-out cell lines.Tests use a paired bootstrap over 237 one-megabase test blocks (one-sided = 0.025). Pilot data. >> Verification. The benchmark target, the window coordinates and the networks equivariance were verified. >> Locus-shared reference. Copying other cell lines measured maps at the same locus matches published Akita on the benchmarks SCC (0.227 vs. 0.230). >> SCC weightings. Two weightings in common use weight distance strata in opposite directions and agree only moderately ({rho} = 0.54). >> Comparison rule. In simulations calibrated on the pilot data, a per-block-best comparison against several baselines has no power. We therefore test against each baseline, which gives [≥] 90 % power at a true gain of 0.02 when between-model correlation is [≥] 0.95. >> H2 positive control. On validation windows, observed maps recover the independent boundaries (AUROC 0.61 - 0.91) and loops (0.86 - 0.90). This fixed the insulation window and showed that these annotations are largely shared across cell types.

preprints.title: Earl Grey ParTEA: scalable, consistent transposable element annotation from pangenomes to deep phylogenetic scopes
preprints.abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) are major drivers of genomic diversity, yet understanding their mobility and functional impact requires their accurate description in genomes. TE annotation is still typically performed genome-by-genome. TEs are often shared between some members of the same or closely related species. Hence, TE annotation with a library from a single reference misses families absent from that assembly, whereas building independent per-genome libraries fails to consistently surface shared TEs, hindering comparison. Here, we present Earl Grey ParTEA, a fully automated Snakemake pipeline extending the functionality of Earl Grey for comparative TE annotation across genome panels. ParTEA builds a single non-redundant TE library from all input genomes, resolves chimeric consensus sequences, and uses this shared library to annotate every genome, enabling direct comparison of TE family diversity, abundance, shared and private content, and activity landscapes. Optional modules provide TE library saturation analysis, BUSCO-based assembly quality control, and phylogenetic ordering of outputs. We applied ParTEA to sets of genomes spanning evolutionary scales: ten Arabidopsis thaliana accessions, ten Drosophila species, and ten species spanning the fungal kingdom. The Drosophila TE library expanded from 343 to 1,852 curated families including a previously missed rolling circle element with over 6,000 copies in D. miranda. The proportion of TE families shared across all genomes was highest within A. thaliana (97.3%), 37.7% across Drosophila species and only 0.5% across the set of fungi. ParTEA is available through Bioconda and represents a computationally efficient reproducible framework for comparative TE analysis in the era of large-scale genome analyses.

preprints.title: Emergence and robustness of 3D complex tissue architectures from simple physical forces
preprints.abstract: Although at central stake in biology and biological engineering, our understanding of how biological tissues acquire their architectures during morphogenesis and which mechanisms have been selected through evolution remain limited. Using adipose tissue as a biological model, we build a 3D mathematical model with simple mechanical rules between cells and fibers, and show that the model reproduces, in-silico, not only the emergence of complex and heterogeneous 3D architectures, but also the intra and inter-individual heterogeneities of shapes as observed in vivo. The model reveals that specific rules for cell differentiation are not necessary for tissue structuring, but could have been selected through evolution for robustness and efficiency. This study therefore suggests a paradigm shift where tissue architecture is an emerging process surprisingly more driven by mechanical processes than by complex predetermined molecular or genetic programs.

last_author.name: Peurichard, D.
last_author.affiliation: Inria Paris

preprints.title: Error-Controlled Discovery of Protein Interactions via Conformal Calibration
preprints.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are powerful predictors of protein interactions, but strong benchmark performance does not ensure reliable discoveries. We introduce PPI-Caliper, a model-agnostic framework that adapts conformal calibration to select interactions at user-specified false discovery rate (FDR) levels using held-out labels without retraining the predictor. Across five species, two PLM-based predictors, and two human training-data versions for each predictor, PPI-Caliper keeps empirical FDR at or below the target level under in-distribution calibration. Under distribution shift, transferred thresholds tend to become conservative when predictive performance improves, but can fail to control FDR when performance deteriorates. PPI-Caliper connects pre-trained interaction scores to explicit error targets and demonstrates why reliable biological discovery requires evaluating calibration alongside predictive accuracy.

last_author.name: Lu, Y. Y.
last_author.affiliation: University of Wisconsin-Madison

preprints.title: FeatureMAP enables network-guided interpretation of untargeted metabolomics
preprints.abstract: Untargeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) metabolomics generates thousands of features, but incomplete metabolite annotation and reliance on predefined pathways limit their biological interpretation. Here we present FeatureMAP, an LC-MS feature-centric computational framework that integrates multi-evidence metabolite annotation, network-guided refinement, metabolic module discovery, and structured large language model-based functional interpretation. Across ten public datasets, FeatureMAP improved MS1-based metabolite candidate prioritization while reducing annotation redundancy. In semi-synthetic benchmarks, FeatureMAP recovered coordinated metabolic perturbations, achieving 92% recovery of a simulated perturbation, and distinguished concurrent metabolic processes. Controlled benchmarks further evaluated functional interpretation under competing metabolite-level signals. Based on FeatureMAP, we additionally developed PhenoMAP, a phenotype-aware knowledge graph comprising 12,929 dysregulated metabolic modules from 501 human metabolomics studies spanning 326 phenotypes. Module-level comparisons revealed reproducible metabolic similarities across independent studies and biologically supported relationships among phenotypes. Application to Alzheimer's disease cerebrospinal fluid and cellular datasets identified convergent membrane-lipid alterations and implicated galactose-linked glycosphingolipid remodeling. Together, FeatureMAP and PhenoMAP enable network-grounded interpretation of incompletely annotated LC-MS metabolomics data and systematic investigation of metabolic dysregulation across biological conditions.

last_author.name: Shen, X.
last_author.affiliation: Nanyang Technological University

preprints.title: FedEpitope: Parameter-Efficient Federated Protein Language Models for Linear B-Cell Epitope Prediction
preprints.abstract: Linear B-cell epitopes are antigenic regions recognised by antibodies that play crucial roles in vaccine development, antibody production, and other therapeutic applications.Their prediction can support peptide-based vaccine candidate screening and diagnostic assay development, but the experimental data required for model development may be distributed across institutions that cannot freely pool their records. We present FedEpitope, a federated framework that adapts the ESM-2 protein language model for peptide-level linear B-cell epitope prediction using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), keeping client-partitioned data local and restricting the communicated trainable model state to approximately 1.11 MB. Simulated benchmarks of FedAvg and FedProx algorithms, evaluated using homology-aware data splits of five biologically heterogeneous, organism-partitioned clients, achieve promising global test performance without centralising training data, with FedAvg outperforming all single-client models in mean AP, F1, and MCC. Additional experiments characterise post-federation personalisation, record-level differential privacy, sensitivity to controlled client heterogeneity, LoRA rank, and generalisation to the independent BCPreds and NetBCE benchmarks, demonstrating the feasibility of parameter-efficient federated protein language model adaptation for data-localised B-cell epitope prediction and the associated trade-offs among predictive performance, personalisation, privacy, communication efficiency, and distribution shift.

preprints.title: Fentanyl and fentanyl-xylazine co-exposure influence mitochondrial transcriptional programs in human trophoblasts
preprints.abstract: Introduction: Illicit fentanyl exposure during pregnancy is associated with adverse outcomes. Yet its direct effects and their underlying molecular mechanisms in human trophoblasts remain largely unknown. Xylazine and medetomidine, two [a]2-adrenergic agonists, were recently detected as adulterants in illicit fentanyl-containing products, and have been linked to worsened clinical outcomes. Methods: We assessed the transcriptional responses of human trophoblast stem (TS) cells in their cytotrophoblast state (TS-CTBs) and derived syncytiotrophoblasts (STBs) after 4-day and 9-day exposure to fentanyl alone or combined with medetomidine and xylazine (FMX). Results: Fentanyl alone produced modest gene expression changes in TS-CTBs, but consistently induced suppression of mitochondrial and ribosomal transcriptional programs in STBs regardless of exposure duration, an effect absent in parental TS-CTBs. 9-day FMX co-exposure influenced mitochondrial respiratory chain gene expression in derived STBs, resulting in discordant regulation of nuclear versus mitochondrial genome-encoded respiratory chain genes. Temporal pathway analysis reveals progressive trophoblast remodeling and dysregulation of mitochondrial transcriptional programs following fentanyl and FMX co-exposure. Discussion: Together, these findings illuminate trophoblast pathways affected by fentanyl alone and by FMX co-exposure, and establish a basis for future studies examining the functional and clinical relevance of these transcriptional responses.

preprints.title: Fertilization offsets the maternal age effect on mouse oocytes provided the oviduct is not itself aged
preprints.abstract: Advanced maternal age compromises oocyte quality, and it is widely assumed that these deficits are transmitted to embryos. However, because most studies rely on in vivo conception, it has been difficult to separate the effects of oocyte aging from those of an aged fertilization environment. In aging mice, we observed that the fraction of ovulated oocytes forming implantation sites after in vivo conception fell ~3.7-fold, raising the question of whether this was due to reduced fertilization, reduced embryo quality or reduced support from the aged reproductive tract. Therefore we fertilized oocytes of aged and young mice in vitro with a shared young-donor sperm preparation, holding the fertilization environment constant and removing paternal variability. Hallmarks of maternal age were largely offset following fertilization in vitro: aged oocytes produced blastocysts at rates comparable to young controls, with altered - but not deficient - cell-lineage composition and no detectable impairment in development to term (E18.5) after transfer to young oviducts. Proteomic analysis revealed that, unlike the transcriptomic signature, the proteomic age signature of oocytes was not faithfully propagated to the blastocyst: for a subset of proteins, particularly those depleted in aged oocytes, the direction of the age effect reversed between oocyte and blastocyst. Comparison with parthenogenetically activated oocytes showed this divergence to be fertilization-dependent, implicating fertilization - rather than mere embryonic cleavage - as the driver of proteomic change. Stable-isotope labelling in live embryos showed that blastocysts from aged, fertilized oocytes both synthesized more new protein and retained less maternal protein than young counterparts; neither effect was detectable after parthenogenesis. Puromycin labelling, by contrast, showed a maternal-age-associated rise in bulk synthesis regardless of route. Together, these results indicate that the maternal-age effect on the oocyte proteome is labile rather than fixed and can be offset by fertilization itself, provided the maternal environment is not itself aged.

preprints.title: Fox: Predicting rates of host-symbiont co-evolution events with association-aware attention
preprints.abstract: Motivation: Hosts and their symbionts share a history of associations in which lineages cospeciate, switch hosts, duplicate, or are lost. Quantifying the relative frequencies of these four events is a central goal of cophylogenetics, but existing tools typically require a fully resolved, correctly rooted host tree, often alongside a symbiont tree, propagating tree-inference errors into the reconciliation and scaling poorly to large systems. Results: We introduce Fox, a transformer neural network architecture that infers the relative frequencies of the four cophylogenetic events directly from a pair of host and symbiont multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) and their sequence mapping, with no tree-reconstruction or reconciliation step. Fox is trained under a simulation-based inference scheme: it learns event frequencies from alignments generated by a coevolutionary process, paying its computational cost once at training time and processing any new system in a single forward pass. On held-out data from its training simulator, Fox recovers event frequencies accurately and with near-zero bias. On additional synthetic data from an independent cophylogeny simulator, its error roughly doubled, but is still very low allowing to track the true frequencies. Most importantly, when compared to the Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC)-based method AmoCoala on these data, it reduces mean absolute error by 45-76% for cospeciations, host switches and duplications and shows similar error for losses, while running more than three orders of magnitude faster. Applied to the empirical cockroach-Blattabacterium system, Fox recovers the expected cospeciation-dominated profile, showing that behaviour learned on simulated data transfers to real sequences. These results confirm that the coevolutionary signal usually extracted from trees can be read directly, accurately, and fast in the alignments themselves

preprints.title: Gene Embedding Hub: a standardized resource for human gene representations
preprints.abstract: Gene embeddings are vector representations of gene identity that provide machine-learning models with information from diverse biological sources. However, their use is hindered by a lack of standardization: inconsistent identifiers, formats, and preprocessing conventions. In this work, we present a unified resource of 67 human gene-embedding sets derived from protein, DNA and RNA sequences, biomedical text, bulk expression data, single-cell expression models, functional data, biological networks, knowledge graphs, regulatory genomics and multimodal models, covering up to 20,097 GENCODE-annotated protein-coding genes. The collection includes both published precomputed embeddings and representations generated or extracted from publicly available models and biological data. Each embedding set is organized in a folder containing the embedding matrix, the Ensembl gene identifiers, machine-readable metadata, and processing documentation. We validate the resource by measuring global and local similarity, cross-embedding consensus, and cross-embedding predictability. The collection is designed to allow community-contributed embeddings that meet predefined technical and documentation requirements, enables comparison of gene representations across modalities and provides standardized embeddings for training and downstream applications.

last_author.name: Boeva, V.
last_author.affiliation: ETH Zurich

preprints.title: Gene regulatory architecture in antibiotic resistance is optimized for specific dynamic regimens
preprints.abstract: Cellular responses to antibiotics face a fundamental trade-off: resistance must be deployed quickly enough to prevent the accumulation of drug inside the cell, but expression of resistance genes is costly in the absence of the drug. Therefore, antibiotic responses are typically regulated, controlling not only whether resistance is expressed, but also when, how strongly, and for how long. These regulatory strategies are implemented through the strength and arrangement of promoters and operators. However, it is still not clear how the dynamics of drug exposure select for specific regulatory strategies. Here, we develop a dynamical model of a typical antibiotic response, where a transcriptional repressor senses the drug and regulates expression of a resistance protein, coupled to the effects of the drug on cell growth and gene expression. We define a cost function that weighs the different burdens imposed on the cell over the course of the response, and perform in silico optimization of the regulatory parameters under different selective pressures for three architectures of increasing complexity: constitutive expression of resistance, repression by a constitutively expressed repressor, and repression by a self-regulated repressor. We find that strong drug exposures favor constitutive expression of resistance, high costs of basal expression favor repression by a constitutive repressor, and self-regulation of the repressor is favored only when the response must provide protection while also restraining overexpression of resistance. Stochastic simulations further show that self-regulation of the repressor protects cells against fluctuations in repressor levels, which cause unnecessary induction of resistance before exposure and failed induction after exposure. This framework links the dynamics of the environment to the evolution of gene regulation, providing a basis to predict which regulatory strategies are expected to arise under specific selective pressures.

last_author.name: Schultz, D.
last_author.affiliation: Dartmouth College

preprints.title: Genome evolution and glycosyltransferase diversification shape asperosaponin biosynthesis in Dipsacus asperoides
preprints.abstract: Deciphering the genomic and enzymatic features associated with high-abundance specialized metabolism is important for understanding and engineering bioactive natural product biosynthesis. Asperosaponin , a hederagenin-based saponin, accumulates at exceptionally high levels in Dipsacus asperoides roots and is by far the predominant triterpenoid saponin. Here, by integrating a chromosome-level genome assembly with comparative genomics, transcriptomics, metabolite profiling, and biochemical characterization, we reconstructed a major biosynthetic route to asperosaponin and identified diversification of triterpenoid-associated gene families. Functional analyses revealed an ordered glycosylation sequence in which DaUGT73GZ2 preferentially accepts C-3-glycosylated substrates retaining a free C-28 carboxyl group, thereby establishing a C-3-before-C-28 glycosylation order during asperosaponin biosynthesis. Phylogenetic and biochemical analyses further uncovered functional differentiation among UGT85CA enzymes involved in C-3 arabinosylation, while genomic and expression analyses revealed lineage-specific patterns of pathway gene duplication and transcriptional regulation. Together, these findings identify genomic, enzymatic, and transcriptional features associated with the distinctive, high-abundance triterpenoid saponin profile of D. asperoides roots and provide a framework for understanding and engineering triterpenoid saponin biosynthesis.

last_author.name: Liang, Y.
last_author.affiliation: Yunnan Agricultural University

preprints.title: GraphExperiment: infrastructure for high-dimensional quantitative data and associated networks in R/Bioconductor
preprints.abstract: Networks are widely used to represent relationships among features (e.g. genes, proteins, and microbial taxa) and among observations (e.g. cells, samples, and species) in omics data, as well as their neighborhoods. The Bioconductor ecosystem provides users and developers with modular and interoperable software tools by relying on standard data structures that are reused across packages. However, Bioconductor lacks a standard data structure to store such networks together with the quantitative data from which they are inferred. Here, we present GraphExperiment, an R/Bioconductor package that provides an S4 class extending SingleCellExperiment with containers for feature- level (rowGraphs) and observation-level (colGraphs) networks stored as igraph objects. Networks are kept in sync with assays, row and column metadata, allowing the simultaneous manipulation of quantitative data and graphs. We demonstrate GraphExperiment in seven use cases covering bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, single-cell proteomics, microbiome, and comparative genomics data, with networks ranging from gene coexpression and protein co-abundance networks to cell-cell communication and phylogenetic networks. GraphExperiment is available on Bioconductor (https://bioconductor.org/packages/GraphExperiment).

last_author.name: Almeida-Silva, F.
last_author.affiliation: Ghent University

preprints.title: Harness engineering enables a multi-agent LLM system to generate cross-domain hypotheses beyond single-investigator reach
preprints.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate scientific hypotheses, and a more capable model is widely assumed to drive output quality. We tested this with a biology-focused multi-agent system coupling an LLM to five Model Context Protocol servers exposing 66 external tools. Upgrading the Synthesizer and Critic from Claude Sonnet 4.6 to Opus 4.8 initially appeared to improve quality, count, and reliability. Under a fully matched harness (identical prompts, schema, hypothesis count, and queries), the differences vanished: scores were indistinguishable on an iPSC-reprogramming task and favoured Sonnet 4.6 on a CHO cell-line-engineering task (18.4 vs 17.4; Welch t = 2.89, p < 0.05). The dominant, controllable driver of quality is therefore the prompting harness, not the model tier. We then introduce the ABCD-Stack (contract-gated prompting, diversity-first generation, adversarial refinement, and cross-family evaluation), which builds these properties in as architecture and shifts outputs toward explicitly falsifiable, causally framed hypotheses beyond the reach of a single-domain investigator. The hypotheses are falsifiable by construction but not yet experimentally validated.

preprints.title: Harnessing catalytic knowledge to guide enzyme discovery and evolution with AlphaEnzyme
preprints.abstract: Retrieving an enzyme for a target reaction provides a starting point for evolution, but predicting how to improve it remains difficult. This requires connecting evolutionary information with the structural and chemical context of catalysis. Here we present AlphaEnzyme, an enzyme foundation model built on a structure-grounded representation of an enzyme paired with its reaction, from which catalytic compatibility, kinetics and mutational response are read out together. On a time-separated benchmark, AlphaEnzyme achieves a top-1 catalyst retrieval success rate of 30.1%, against 17.2% for the strongest baseline. Michaelis constant predictions achieve the highest rank correlations among the compared methods, reaching 0.64 for enzymes sharing at most 40% identity with the kinetic training set. The model also enriches high-fitness TrpB variants at a budget of 16 candidates without target-specific fitness training. In prospective transaminase engineering, several prioritized variants exceed the parent, with the best design yielding a 30.4-fold increase in product signal in a lysate-based assay while retaining (R)-selectivity. Together, AlphaEnzyme provides a common molecular basis for selecting starting enzymes and prioritizing sequence changes for their improvement.

last_author.name: Zheng, S.
last_author.affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University

preprints.title: Improving real-time search through deep learning-enhanced fragment ion indexing
preprints.abstract: The fragment ion indexed database searching approach enables highly efficient tandem mass spectrometry database searches, including real-time search workflows. However, the index can require tens of gigabytes of memory, often exceeding the free memory available on instrument acquisition computers running the search. This restricts the size of the searchable database, the variable modification space, and the number of searches that can run concurrently. To address this problem, we developed an index-pruning pipeline within the Comet database search tool using Carafe, a deep learning tool that predicts fragment ion intensities based on peptide sequences. In our approach, only fragment ion positions that are predicted to be observable are written in the index, eliminating entries that are unlikely to contribute to spectrum detection. We evaluated this approach on two search spaces in three index configurations to demonstrate that masking significantly reduced the number of fragment ion index entries and, consequently, peak search memory use. Masked searches were also faster than unmasked searches and identified a comparable number of peptide-spectrum matches. Because all prediction and masking steps are performed before searching, their cost is amortized across repeated, future searches of the same database and modification configuration, introducing no per-spectrum search overhead. The complete implementation is open source with an Apache license.

preprints.title: Kontext: Kernel-based method bridging spatial domain identification and cell-cell communication
preprints.abstract: The spatial organization of biological tissues is characterized by spatial domains: regions with coherent transcriptional and anatomical properties, heavily influenced by local cell-cell interactions. Although identifying spatial domains is a common task in spatial transcriptomics, most existing methods provide limited mechanistic insight into their organization. We present Kontext, a kernel-based framework that jointly represents cells and their local environments, enabling the identification of spatial domains grounded in their underlying ligand-receptor interactions. This representation further provides complementary outputs for characterizing cellular microenvironments, spatial niches, and sender-receiver communication patterns. Kontext outperforms state-of-the-art methods in recovering reference domain annotations across several spatial transcriptomics technologies and biological models, while offering improved computational efficiency and scalability. Applying Kontext on a Xenium temporal mouse heart cryoinjury dataset, we characterize the spatiotemporal evolution of the injury and identify an undescribed sustained activity of the complement system in the communication between fibroblasts and macrophages during scar maturation. In a million-cell three-dimensional Open-ST dataset of human metastatic lymph node tissue, we combine spatial domain identification and niche analysis to define the boundary region between the tumor and its microenvironment, revealing distinct communication patterns between this interface and the tumor core.

last_author.name: Cantini, L.
last_author.affiliation: CNRS and Institut Pasteur

preprints.title: LIMBER: A Hybrid RNA Foundation Model for Predicting and Understanding RNA Structure and Function
preprints.abstract: RNA foundation models offer a promising route to decoding the relationships between RNA sequence, structure and function, yet how model shapes the acquisition and organization of biological information remains poorly understood. Here we introduce Layer-Interleaved Mamba-Bidirectional Encoder for RNA (LIMBER), a hybrid foundation model integrating bidirectional self-attention with selective state-space modeling, pretrained on 40.5 million non-coding RNA sequences. Through task-specific fine-tuning, LIMBER achieves leading performance on secondary-structure prediction and non-coding RNA classification benchmarks, while demonstrating strong transferability to translation-related tasks and RNA--small-molecule interaction prediction. Beyond model development, we establish a unified, task-agnostic framework to systematically evaluate and interpret the biological knowledge intrinsically acquired by RNA foundation models. This framework validates LIMBER's strong capabilities in recovering RNA structures and predicting mutational effects, while uncovering a hierarchical, task-dependent organization of different biological information across model layers. By further systematically training and evaluating a broad panel of model variants spanning model capacity, training duration and dataset size, we uncover distinct scaling behaviors across structural, evolutionary and functional capabilities. Together, these findings establish LIMBER as a versatile RNA foundation model and provide broader insights into how architectural design, internal representations and scaling shape the learning of RNA sequence-structure-function relationships.

preprints.title: LPT: Orchestrating bounded agentic loops for automated protein binder design
preprints.abstract: Current large language models (LLMs) can reason over scientific information and use code-based tools, but their training knowledge is broad rather than specialized, can be out of date and is hard to attribute to sources. Furthermore, unconstrained agentic workflows and unlimited tool use can consume large amounts of tokens. Here we present LPT (little protein tiger), a framework for fixed orchestration of LLM stages, each running a bounded agentic loop with custom system prompts and tool access, to enable de novo protein binder design from a single natural language prompt. The LLM stages can query a curated literature database, containing ~14000 papers digested into key findings, enabling recall of specialized information. An LLM with database access answered 41/48 test questions drawn from database key findings correctly, while a model without access answered none. In three end-to-end design campaigns, initiated from a single prompt, LPT autonomously identified the design intent, selected targets, structures and hotspot residues and designed candidate binders to disrupt CALCRL/RAMP1, PD-1/PD-L1 and PVR-TIGIT interactions. Cross-validation with multiple folding models confirms a high in silico success rate at minimal token consumption and low computational costs.

last_author.name: Uckelmann, M.
last_author.affiliation: Hubrecht Institute

preprints.title: Language-guided domain adaptation improves protein sequence rep-resentations for antimicrobial resistance analysis
preprints.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR), particularly antibiotic resistance in bacterial pathogens, complicates infectious disease management. Because bacterial resistance is often mediated by protein functions, including antibiotic inactivation and efflux, protein sequence analysis provides a molecular basis for digital AMR surveillance and therapeutic intervention. We developed BacLLM, a language guided protein representation framework that integrates annotation-derived functional knowledge into protein language model representations for AMR analysis in WHO priority bacterial pathogens. Through sequence enhancement, semantic enrichment of UniProt annotations, and cross modal contrastive learning, BacLLM transfers LLM encoded annotation priors into the sequence encoder. Compared with baselines, BacLLM provided more informative representations for resistance-gene identification and mechanism prediction, captured resistance associated mutational signals at single-residue resolution, and preserved taxonomic relationships not reflected by phenotype based clinical groupings. Moreover, BacLLM recovered resistance associated functional organization within a TolC-centered protein association network, prioritizing proteins with low sequence identity to TolC but predicted structural similarity to TolC. Extending from AMR characterization to therapeutic prioritization, BacLLM also improved strain-level phage host matching for phage therapy candidate prioritization. Together, these findings establish BacLLM as a protein representation framework supporting AMR surveillance, functional characterization, and therapeutic candidate prioritization.

preprints.title: Leakage-Controlled Benchmarking of Variant Effect Predictors and Development of Gradient-Boosting Consensus Model
preprints.abstract: Single amino acid mutations are among the most common forms of genetic variation, with effects ranging from negligible to severe disruption of protein function. Accurate quantitative evaluation of protein variants therefore represents a key challenge in medicine and protein engineering. Computational variant effect predictors (VEPs) are widely used to prioritize missense variants, yet their fair comparison is hindered by data circularity, benchmarks restricted to human clinical annotations, and limited availability of code and training data, all of which can inflate apparent performance. Here, we reviewed 18 recent and 3 older, widely adopted variant effect predictors for reproducible benchmarking and assembled a rigorously curated, leakage-controlled Benchmark dataset by integrating clinically annotated human variants from ClinVar and Humsavar as well as cross-species variants with functional annotations. The evaluation on this dataset revealed a narrow overall performance range for the benchmarked tools (AUC 0.631-0.758) and a consistent drop from clinical to functional data. Surprisingly, several tools published two decades ago demonstrated comparable performance to mid-ranked modern predictors. Building on these results, we developed a gradient-boosting consensus model, PredictSNPprot, which achieved an AUC of 0.82 on a held-out test set, outperforming the original PredictSNP meta-predictor and the best individual state-of-the-art tool by 13.6 and 5.7 percentage points, respectively. The Benchmark dataset, including the predictions from the evaluated tools, is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23597130 and PredictSNPprot consensus predictor is available at https://github.com/loschmidt/PredictSNPprot.

preprints.title: Light-dependent conversion of body color change pattern during zebrafish development
preprints.abstract: Zebrafish (Danio rerio) shows body color change in response to light: when light comes, it whitens body color. Our previous study has shown that larval zebrafish as early as 5 days post-fertilization (dpf) have this capacity fully developed whereas 2-dpf larvae exhibit light-induced darkening in sharp contrast (Shiraki et al. 2010). Here, we discovered that the conversion in body color change pattern between 2 dpf and 5 dpf is light-dependent: larvae reared in darkness exhibited light-induced darkening of body color, reminiscent of 2-dpf larvae. We also found that a 14-h light exposure on 3 or 4 dpf is sufficient to trigger this conversion, and that the conversion by light on 4 dpf still occurred after ablation of most exorh-expressing pineal photoreceptor cells. The dark-reared larvae had significantly lower transcription levels of pmch and pmchl, which encode melanin-concentrating hormone precursors, than the LD-reared larvae. However, the levels in larvae that had undergone the conversion (3-L and 4-L) were not significantly different from those in dark-reared larvae, indicating that the reduced pmch/pmchl expression alone does not account for the conversion. In conclusion, light exposure in rearing is indispensable for the maturation of body color change ability in larval zebrafish through a regulatory mechanism independent of exorh-expressing pineal photoreceptors.

last_author.name: Kojima, D.
last_author.affiliation: University of Tokyo

preprints.title: Marker-specific pixel attribution for single-cell protein quantification with PixAQ
preprints.abstract: Imaging mass cytometry (IMC) typically quantifies all markers within the same cell mask, although their signals have distinct spatial distributions. This quantification method may omit relevant signals or include signals from neighboring cells. We present PixAQ, which improves single-cell protein quantification in IMC through marker-specific probabilistic pixel attribution. PixAQ combines spatial proximity with anchor-group intensity models to assign pixel-marker observations among neighboring cells and an explicit residual component. Original intensities are averaged over marker-specific supports. Across three cohorts (680 regions), comparisons in 366 patients showed improved agreement with predefined population-marker relationships, with cohort-median patient-paired gains of 1.99 to 4.83 percentage points in expected-marker share over shared-mask quantification. Ablation analyses showed that both spatial and intensity evidence contributed to these gains. Conventional and high-resolution IMC images linked supports to visible local and intracellular signal structures. PixAQ improves single-cell protein quantification by determining which local signals contribute to each marker measurement without changing cell segmentation.

preprints.title: MicrobeRT: A Framework and Suite of Fine-tuned Language Models for Genomic Sequences
preprints.abstract: Accurate and reproducible metagenomic analysis is essential for effective infectious disease surveillance. Targeted diagnostics such as culturing, antigen assays, and multiplex PCR panels identify only predefined organisms and can fail to identify atypical or novel infections. Shotgun metagenomics offers hypothesis-free detection, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity, dependence on mutable reference databases, and high computational cost. To combat these challenges, we introduce MicrobeRT, an integrated suite of genomic language models fine-tuned to classify metagenomic sequencing reads across three tasks: (i) species level taxonomic identification, (ii) antibiotic resistance gene detection, and (iii) pathogenicity assessment. The framework builds on three pre-trained genomic language models - Nucleotide Transformer (Dalla-Torre et al 2025), DNABERT (Ji et al 2021, Zhou et al 2024), and HyenaDNA (Nguyen et al 2024) - leveraging their large-scale genomic pre-training, adaptability to downstream tasks, and, in the case of HyenaDNA, ability to capture long-range sequence dependencies. The models are fine-tuned on large, curated datasets spanning microbial, viral, fungal, and human genomes, including more than 500,000 genomes and 250,000 antibiotic resistance gene sequences. To evaluate the performance of our fine-tuned genomic language models across classification tasks, we developed a benchmarking framework that compares MicrobeRT against state-of-the-art (SOTA) bioinformatics tools. Across both simulated and empirical datasets, the models achieve strong performance while reducing computational overhead. MicrobeRT is released as open-source software, enabling further fine-tuning and reproducible integration of alternative models and classifiers. We also demonstrate seamless, drop-in integration by incorporating our fine-tuned taxonomic classification models as an optional add-on within the open-source TaxTriage pipeline (Merritt et al 2026). MicrobeRT demonstrates the feasibility of three clinically relevant multi-label analyses, offering a practical path to scalable, reproducible metagenomic diagnostics and enabling broader deployment of AI/ML-enhanced infectious disease testing.

preprints.title: MorphoProt: RNA-Conditioned Integration of Multiscale Histology for Spatial Protein Inference
preprints.abstract: Spatially resolved protein abundance reveals cellular states and tissue organization that RNA expression cannot fully capture, yet direct spatial protein profiling remains costly and limited in coverage. Histology images routinely accompany spatial transcriptomics and offer complementary morphological information for protein inference. Here, we introduce MorphoProt, a multimodal framework that jointly predicts spatial protein abundance from RNA expression, multiscale histology and tissue neighborhoods. MorphoProt uses RNA-guided cross-attention over five histological fields of view, so that the morphological context read for each spot is conditioned on its molecular state. The fused representation is refined by gated aggregation of RNA-derived information from physical and transcriptomic neighborhoods before joint protein prediction. On held-out sections of human tonsil, mouse spleen and human liver, MorphoProt achieves mean proteinwise Spearman correlations of 0.652, 0.604 and 0.372, outperforming matched RNA-only and graph-based baselines and the histology-based HIPI and multimodal SPRINT baselines in all three tissues. Combining fields of view, rather than any single one, carries the histology gain: in spleen and liver, the multiscale model outperforms every single-field model, and its learned scale preference separates white-pulp from red-pulp compartments. Predicted proteins preserve protein-defined tissue domains and their marker identity, and recover pathologist-annotated germinal centers as accurately as measured proteins.
